Key aspects of the paper include the formulation of the control problem, its weak formulation, a priori error estimation for a particular numerical discretization, and a hybrid model using the Monte-Carlo method. It also explores a more efficient simulation-based solution using the stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method. In addition to these findings, the paper demonstrates the efficacy of a hybrid model that combines the Monte-Carlo method and the finite element method used for spatial discretization. It further provides an interesting application of this hybrid model to a real-world problem involving the simulation of a random velocity field in a control problem with the Navier-Stokes equation as the evolutionary equation, along with an observation on the computational costs of this simulation. It also highlights some open problems in this field of research. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate and rule out potential experimental errors, our approach was refined, and we employed multiple detectors to re-analyze the data, still discovering the anisotropy to be quite evident. Furthermore, we observed that this anisotropy persists across various energy intervals above 4 EeV, with the anisotropy's overall magnitude appearing to increase with energy. The orientation of the anisotropy's dipole axis shows some variation but generally points towards the direction of the Large Atlantics Galaxy Cluster. The observed anisotropy patterns also exhibit a degree of complexity, with some indications of bi-modal structure. These findings underscore the notion that extremely energetic cosmic rays are capable of carrying intricate information regarding their sources and the environments through which they travel. The substantial size of the anisotropy patterns themselves - extending over $21.5^{\circ}$ in right ascension - also merits particular attention. The most plausible explanation for these findings is related to distribution patterns of massive galactic systems, rather than intrinsic properties of the cosmic rays themselves. The observed patterns of anisotropy also offer a compelling rationale for conducting focused searches for identical anisotropy signals in corresponding energy ranges detected by other extremely energetic cosmic ray observatories, such as the Telescope Array. The extensive energy range and anisotropy patterns observable with our experiment also lend support to theories suggesting that extremely energetic cosmic rays can be used as 'light' to illuminate distant structures, far beyond the observable universe. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies that employed similar frameworks. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative method for handling functional dependencies with null values, (b) a data condition validation algorithm, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to existing research on data merging and quality assessment. Elevated levels of data inconsistency are addressed in the paper, along with suggestions for further development. We anticipate that our research will contribute significantly to handling inconsistencies in data tables.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in three dimensions. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. These updated results agree with three-dimensional renormalization group calculations and indicate that the edge singularity's location is less sensitive to $N$ than previously thought, with an estimated scaling dimension of 2.4 to 2.7 along the critical line. These findings support using $z_c \approx 1.6$ as a universal value to $N$ of 2, 4,  $\ldots$. We develop a key estimation tool for peaked random structures in the context of statistical mechanics and combinatorial optimization, building upon the Sudakov-Fernique superconcave function. This tool is used to demonstrate the superconcave nature of the TAP free energy near its peak, providing an alternative to previous proofs of local convexity. As a result of this approach, we gain insight into the non-convexity of the TAP free energy in the regime far from the peak and offer a contrast to the locally convex region found using Poincaré-Sobolev inequalities in Bernoulli mean-field spin glasses. Our research also yields an estimate of the width of the non-convex region in the TAP free energy landscape. Notably, we find that this width grows proportionally to the square root of the system size when the optimization problem in question is uncorrelated and has a bounded second moment. This finding differs from the exponential growth observed in previous studies of uncorrupted systems, suggesting that the introduced measure of disorder size does not capture the complexity of the optimization problem at hand and implying that the associated combinatorial landscape is locally landscape-rugged. This notion is supported by a related result stating that the TAP free energy landscape becomes globally rugged in a system of infinite size. Our approach to analyzing the TAP free energy landscape involves a stochastic analysis of the replica, which yields an analog of the Poincaré-Sobolev inequality for Gaussian processes with a specific covariance function. This inequality is used to demonstrate the superconcave nature of the Sudakov-Fernique function, and by extension, the TAP free energy landscape. As a standalone result, we also obtain an estimate of the expected squared norm of the derivative of a random Gaussian polynomial evaluated at a random point, which may have independent interest in the context of statistical physics and combinatorial optimization, as well as in the broader realm of stochastic analysis. This estimate is obtained through a stochastic version of the Poincaré-Sobolev inequality, which is established by applying a variant of the Banach algebra technique used in previous studies of the TAP free energy landscape. This variant involves a stochastic version of the Riesz-Thorin interpolation theorem, the Helton's interpolation theorem, and the Banach algebra technique used to obtain the Poincaré-Sobolev inequality for the standard Gaussian measure. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to group overlapping heatmaps, facilitating efficient pose candidates. Furthermore, a correspondence learning module is proposed to enhance the robustness of the prediction model by training it to differentiate between valid and artificial correspondences. We tested the proposed framework, named DeepHMap++, on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. Code has been made publicly available at: https://github.com/zhengyangyin/DeepHMap++.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. The library utilizes SciPy for optimization and provides Python functions to handle data preprocessing and post-estimation analysis. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/USAJohnson/GGLasso. The package is suited for large-scale sparse inverse covariance estimation in a range of applications, including genomics and finance. The associated R package is RCGGLasso. Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. To this end, the relationship between the methods, their precision in configurational averaging, and the underlying biology of molecules is discussed. In particular, the average precision of commonly employed methods in biology is calculated and insights are provided to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of molecular simulations. In these simulations, issues with peptide bonds can be addressed by modifying the methods used to numerically integrate the equations. In this context, the L\"{o}werrys-Sorter method and its variants, including the Langevin dynamics method used in molecular dynamics simulations, the v-reduced method, the modified v-reduced method, the BCF method, the implicit Euler method, and the Brownian dynamics method, among others, are examined and their limitations discussed. Further, the methods that yield precise configurational averages in harmonic oscillators, such as the Langevin dynamics method, are identified and recommendations are made to enhance the accuracy of biomolecular simulations, especially in resolving peptide bonds, by either using the methods that yield precise averages or incorporating harmonic oscillators locally within the simulations. In these scenarios, the methods and their variants can be used to enforce the biological constraints and potentially speed up the simulations by reducing the impact of peptide bonds on the overall dynamics. The paper also highlights the differences between configurational and ergodic averaging and discusses the precision of commonly employed methods in biomolecular simulations, providing a related open-source code. Further, the paper discusses and addresses the issue of ring rotations in proteins, another barrier that biomolecular simulations must overcome, and offers advice on how to tackle it. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer. Unlike traditional eigenvector centrality calculations, the recurrence relation used here takes into account the values from other layers. We show that the eigenvectors in each layer are related through the adjacency matrix's eigenvector equation and propose a hybrid algorithm to compute these values, especially suitable for large networks. By analyzing a real-world airtrans transportation network, we demonstrate that our approach yields meaningful results compared to existing centrality measures. For an idealized example and the airtrans network, we also examine the impact of different $\lambda$ values on the distribution of centrality values. The results indicate that the smallest $\lambda$ value produces distributions most similar to degree centrality, while the largest $\lambda$ value yields distributions most similar to traditional eigenvector centrality. The proposed algorithm's efficiency is demonstrated through a comparison with the brute-force hybrid approach. The proposed multilayer eigenvector centrality algorithm can be applied to a wide range of complex network analysis applications. The code associated with this research is publicly available on GitHub. The proposed algorithm was able to effectively tackle networks with a limited number of layers but large numbers of nodes and edges. The results obtained suggest that the effectiveness of the algorithm can be improved by either decreasing the number of layers or reducing the $\lambda$ value in each layer. Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the $R$-Minkowski representation. This approach enables us to employ the method of 
separation of variables originally proposed by Fock. Ultimately, we present some specific 
solutions to the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime. These solutions can be 
interpreted as massless solutions since they are devoid of singularities that could arise 
from the introduction of a finite speed of light, and these solutions also match the 
results obtained using other methods. We then introduce external electromagnetic and scalar 
fields into the $R$-Minkowski spacetime and demonstrate how they affect the Dirac equation 
and its solutions. We also derive the classical field equations for these fields, which 
are in accordance with well-known theories. We then propose a new quantum field theory, 
based on the $R$-Minkowski spacetime, which includes non-linear connections and covariant 
derivative operators that define the Dirac operator. This new operator is used to derive 
the Heisenberg uncertainty principle in its original form, and it also provides a new 
interpretation of the Casimir effect. We then discuss some open problems that arise in 
this context. We believe that the $R$-Minkowski spacetime offers vast possibilities for 
developing new theories and interpreting physical phenomena, and as such, it represents 
a valuable contribution to the advancement of theoretical physics. We also outline a 
potential path for developing a quantum gravity theory based on the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra, 
and we provide some numerical solutions to the Dirac equation within the de Sitter 
spacetime. We conclude by examining the relationship between the Fock coordinate 
transformation and the de Sitter spacetime, and we demonstrate that the de Sitter 
spacetime corresponds to a specific, flat $R$-Minkowski spacetime when viewed from an 
observer located at its center.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. A comprehensive set of high-speed cameras recordings, covering a broad spectrum of impact velocities, informs and expands the current understanding of these water-entry interactions. A parameter called "deep-pinched" was introduced to distinguish between water-entrapment and surface-seal interactions, and various stages of water-entry interactions are illustrated in an appendix table for easy reference. A notorious "turbulent stage" Pinch-off Time (PT) model's inaccuracy at mid-range speeds is also highlighted, suggesting that a more complex model incorporating factors like pressure and water-entrapment depth is necessary to accurately capture the pinch-off times of spheres that experience this "turbulent stage". A discussion on the "deep-pinched" parameter and water-entrapment interactions, complete with an accompanying water-entrapment stage table, and a "turbulent stage" PT model's limitations are also presented. A set of supplementary movies is available on the Cambridge University Knowledge-Live platform, along with the underlying data for the main figures, and an open-source code for the "turbulent stage" PT model. A broader context for this research, encompassing its potential applications, and a list of key terms used throughout the study are also provided. A study on the dynamics of water-entry interactions at mid-range speeds, complete with an integrated analysis and an in-depth examination of the pressure and water-entrapment depth influences, is proposed as future work. A list of references that informed and guided this study is included for further review. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. By approximating the cubanite crystal lattice, we also find that the unique properties of this compound are insensitive to external pressures and lateral distortions of the lattice. Consequently, we suggest that cubanite is an ideal candidate to explore novel phases of matter that arise from the interplay between strong correlation and strong spin-orbit effects. This can be achieved either through applied pressure or lattice defects that introduce asymmetry. Experimental verification of our predictions is feasible through various means including resonant soft X-ray scattering, anomalous finish electron microscopy, and inelastic neutron scattering. This compound holds significant value for the broader community as it relates to our ongoing efforts to develop theories of orbital selectivity seen in certain compounds featuring 3d transition metals, often under external pressure or with asymmetrical lattice distortions. In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. This process can be applied to both the 3+1 spacetime dimensions and the 4+1 spacetime dimensions using complex geometry. We also provide a comprehensive explanation of the complex differential calculation to obtain the complex coefficients of the Ricci tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Additionally, we offer a concise introduction to both the basic concepts and advanced applications of the Newman-Penrose formalism. This work is intended for undergraduate students and research scholars in the fields of physics and mathematics. A notable feature of this review is the use of simple and intuitive graphical representations to illustrate the complex differential calculations and the underlying geometry. These explanations can also be found in the appendices of this review. We hope this work will serve as an inspiration for both undergraduate and graduate level courses that incorporate the Newman-Penrose formalism. A notable research area that is not covered in this review is the complex conformal structure. It is characterized by a distinct set of complex differential equations involving the Weyl tensor, which serves as a critical component in the analysis of complex conformal structures. It is also worth mentioning that this review is not a comprehensive summary of the numerous solutions to Einstein's field equations using the Newman-Penrose formalism that have been derived in the context of complex conformal structures. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more efficient and clinically relevant approach that involves combining the feed and the endoscopic findings with the CT scans. We used a Dense Dense Unet model with two separate input streams for the CT images and the fusion of the feed and endoscopic findings, and evaluated its performance on a newly created dataset consisting of 200 cases. The results show that the model's ability to identify lesions in the upper part of the esophagus is reduced compared to its performance on lower esophageal lesions. This finding's underlying cause requires further investigation but it may be related to the anatomy of the esophagus. With some pre-processing of the images, the model achieved an Dice similarity coefficient of over 0.87 for all lesions and it was possible to use a low resolution of 128x128x32 for the esophageal tumor segmentation from the CT images. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To address this challenge, researchers employed time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, researchers have also determined that both the effects of local fields and spin-orbit interactions are vital to correctly determining the energy loss of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Lastly, further validating the $\gamma$-Ta$_2$O$_5$ structure, researchers employed a Monte Carlo method to compare calculated reflection loss spectra with the actual results of experiments, achieving a very accurate match. These findings suggest that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase is the ground state of the material, representing a crystalline arrangement that is both stable and safe as it does not have any unusual or exotic characteristics that could make it hazardous. This research has also highlighted the incredible diversity present within Ta$_2$O$_5$, underscoring the importance of further investigation to determine the potential unique properties of its various forms. Ultimately, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of Ta$_2$O$_5$, a complex and multifaceted material that is certain to guide any future analyses of this compound.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. These findings support the hypothesis that the large-scale geographical sorting of Americans may contribute to the spread of online misinformation. We also identified varying levels of misinformation dissemination in different regions, with areas with closed social networks and high trust in their communities exhibiting higher levels of dissemination. These results have implications for the understanding of The Big Sort and suggest that combating online misinformation requires approaches that address the segmentation of society. Within this framework, we systematically explore QFT complexity, detailing its key properties such as monotonicity, boundary terms, and additivity, all at the cost of introducing a degree of ambiguity. Notably, we demonstrate that the geometric formulation inherently resists the challenges posed by trigonometric boundary conditions and 2D conformal transformations. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. With the advent of big data analytics, user-generated content has exploded, making recommendation systems for social media platforms increasingly challenging. With over 1.9 billion active users on YouTube, the need for a efficient recommender system with an expansive knowledge base has never been more pressing. We apply MSDCR to the YouTube dataset, thereby setting a new benchmark for future research. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/songjunhui/Multi-Sparse-Domain-Recommendation.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The implementation of Hypatia is accompanied by examples of its capabilities, including accessible code that can be used as a starting point for further development. The project is also hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/JuliaOpt/Hypatia. The JuliaOpt group is responsible for maintaining the project. The proposed method is suitable for a wide range of applications and research related to interior-point methods, JuMP, and exotic cones. It can be used as a starting point for further analysis and development of more advanced and complex projects. The conic solver Hypatia is designed to handle complex geometric shapes that have a circular cross-section. It can also handle shapes with multiple connected components. The project provides pre-defined exotic cones including but not limited to: indicator cones, quartenary cones, tridiagonal cones, and circular cones. The JuMP framework is a high-level abstract representation of the problems that can be solved with Hypatia. The framework provides an interface for problem formulation and control over the solution process. The development of Hypatia is done using Julia, a high-performance, high-productivity, general-purpose, multi-paradigm programming language. The language is designed to be efficient, with the ability to compile code to native machine code. The implementation of Hypatia uses Julia's built-in functionality, JuMP, and the Mosek solver. The project includes examples of convex optimization problems that can be solved with Hypatia, including problems that use the tridiagonal cone, the circular cone, and the binary indicator cone. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across novel, unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps, expanding the standard pipeline with additional processing of PHIP images, quality assessment, and robust signal extraction. We analyzed nine different combinations of preprocessing, feature extraction, and machine learning approaches to enable efficient generalization, drawing from a wide range of methods including deep learning techniques, principal components, and robust regression. Results showed modest gains from expanding the MRIQC pipeline through additional preprocessing and feature extraction but little improvement from feature reduction and machine learning methods. Ultimately, we established a optimized pipeline that yielded 0.02 lower AUROC and 0.03 lower AUPRC on the ABIDE validation set and the CATI-derived datasets, respectively. This optimized pipeline is valuable for a wide range of MRI studies and provides a foundational framework for further generalization testing and development of a more advanced pipeline. The study's findings and methodology are accessible through an interactive dashboard hosted on NeuroVault. The MRIQC pipeline's code and results are available on GitHub. The derived CATI dataset is accessible via the OpenNeuro platform. The ABIDE preprocessed dataset is available for download on the ABIDE website. The MRIQC project, including the code and results, the derived CATI dataset, and the ABIDE preprocessed dataset, can be accessed through the MRIQC website. The study was conducted in collaboration with the MRIQC working group. The code for the optimized pipeline and the analysis dashboard can be found on GitHub. This research investigates how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages. A significant surge in EV adoption is anticipated, which will affect how distributors manage and recover their systems. Our study utilizes a novel three-layer optimization framework to analyze the situation and recommends a course of action for grid operators, drivers, and EV owners. The framework separates individual EV owner charging decisions from collective actions taken by the distribution system operator in response to grid issues. Our key discovery indicates that, to boost grid resilience, distributors should focus on recovering specific sections of the grid where there are high concentrations of EVs and charge freely. This can be achieved at a minimal financial cost by offering incentives to EV owners to charge their vehicles. Our research incorporates real-world data and grid management challenges. Our findings show that a simple 'charge free' policy for EVs located near each other can significantly cut recovery costs by 20-50% and even 60-70% in cases where there are grid frequency issues. Our analysis also reveals that the best outcome occurs when EV owners prioritize public charging stations over private ones. This reduces recovery costs by as much as 50-70% more. Our research addresses key challenges in modeling and analyzing EV-related issues and provides a straightforward 'charge free' policy as a valuable contribution. This policy can be used by distributors as a starting point to better understand the benefits of free public charging for grid resilience and can also be used by EV owners and manufacturers as a valuable tool to manage and promote free public charging. This research was conducted using a real-world Australian test bed but is applicable to any region with a similar power grid management system. Our findings suggest that free public charging can reduce grid issues and even push it towards stability. This is a significant discovery that challenges existing beliefs and provides a new perspective on managing EV-related issues. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Consequently, this research provides a novel example where a rendezvous scenario among multiple autonomous agents exhibits chaotic properties, a phenomenon observed previously only in scenarios involving a single autonomous entity. The expanded framework also offers valuable insights into the underlying dynamics of these encounters, allowing for targeted modifications to create a more stable and predictable meeting point, as well as facilitating the integration of additional autonomous entities into the system with relative ease. The development of a straightforward, efficient control mechanism for motivating the agents to adhere to this new meeting point is a significant advancement offered by this paper, with benefits extending beyond the rendezvous scenario to any application involving autonomous decision-making under the Motivation Dynamics framework. The inclusion of a rendezvous scenario among three or more autonomous entities meeting at a single point is also a novel contribution presented in this paper, offering a rich and complex pattern of interacting agents that is responsive to changes and exhibits both local and global patterns of behavior. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. This novel approach remains a promising line of investigation that can be tested with the upcoming AFOSearch and LSST observational datasets. Given its own inherent uncertainties, we recommend future investigations that might further clarify several crucial aspects, including but not limited to: assessing the impact of lensing effects on SN Ia samples selected based on the stretch versus colour diagram, combining the effects of lensing with those of external standardization, and calculating the effects of lensing on SN Ia light curves that can, in turn, influence the selected estimator calculations. Given these considerations, we propose an open-access Python code called SNMag, which calculates the additional dispersion in SN Ia magnitude due to weak lensing convergence. This code can be used by individual researchers who, in turn, are encouraged to contribute their own research findings back to the community. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. To further investigate the relationship between T center formation and device layer depth, we implemented a sensitive measurement of the carrier-enforcement of the 1.67eV transition, and discovered a previously unreported 'deep T' center with an ~10x greater density compared to its 'interface T' counterpart, presenting significant implications for the development of quantum devices that rely on multiple T center levels. With the ability to tailor device layer depths and depth profiles of the T center densities, our results also demonstrate the feasibility of further optimizing the migration length of the interface T centers in search of extended spin coherence times. To bring this research one step closer to practical device fabrication, we designed a series of wafer bonding SOI structures and demonstrated the compatibility of T centers with photonic integration, setting the stage for the development of quantum interface devices that combine multiple levels of T centers with nanophotonic elements. With the ability to grow a thin layer of oxide directly on T centers, we were also able to explore the effects of carrier screening on the transition energies of the interface and deep T centers, discovering a previously unreported 'buried T' center that could provide even greater levels of spectral diffusion. With an eye on the long-term goals of quantum device integration, we conclude by discussing the potential of T centers in a 'quantum silicon stack' architecture, where multiple levels of T centers are combined with nanowire interfaces and a thin layer of oxide, presenting a promising pathway for the development of a universal quantum interface device. The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain condition $\beta\in [0,2)$; here $m$ denotes a function that belongs to Kirchhoff type, $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$, and there is a function $h_i\in \left(\big(H^1_0(\Omega)\big)^*,\|\cdot\|_*\right)$. By making use of a singular Trudinger-Moser inequality for a small positive value $\varepsilon$ and variational methods, we are able to establish sufficient conditions for a multiplicity of the system's solutions given the given conditions. Additionally, by changing one of the $f_i$ to $e^u$, we can derive an original result about the system's solutions. This research builds on previous work done by Liang and Yang in 2018. A single equation with the same characteristics was previously investigated by Liang and Yang in 2018, and by Jiao and Yang in 2019. A system without the Kirchhoff term was previously examined by Yang and Jiao in 2019, and by Chen, souplet, and Vaira in 2020. A singular Trudinger-Moser inequality was used in all of these studies. This research can be found in the journal Advances in Nonlinear Analysis, volume 9, number 1, 2020. Another related paper is also mentioned. We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our goal is to analyze how the variance of a given function affecting the vectors influences their expected behavior. This connection is captured through specific concentration inequalities, with the strengths of these inequalities varying based on whether the underlying distribution exhibits SCP or SRP characteristics. Notably, when distributions exhibit SRP, we establish that the function's expectation remains bounded by a constant times its square root, an outcome that surpasses previous analogues. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the minimal value of the function's variance, applicable to both SCP and SRP settings. This lower bound serves as a necessary condition for distributions to demonstrate negative dependence characteristics. Furthermore, we offer a lower bound for the expected value of the absolute difference between pairs of randomly selected binary variables, providing a criterion that must be met for any distribution yielding negative dependence. This condition essentially defines strong anti-concentration distributions, a new and distinguishing feature of which is that it includes discrete uniform distributions over odd-sized sets. We also establish a variety of sharp subgaussian inequalities for both SCP and SRP settings, concluding with an exploration of these results' applications to statistical estimation problems. These applications involve both standard maximum likelihood estimation and Bayesian estimation frameworks. We demonstrate the positive impact of considering strong anti-concentration distributions, which allows for the successful estimation of certain models that, when attempted using previous approaches, would fail to converge. These models include the underlying parameter of a Bayesian network, as well as the distribution of a discrete parameter from a Bayesian distribution. We provide a strategy for extending our concentration inequalities to Bayesian estimation contexts by generating strong anti-concentration distributions from combinations of the original distributions used to generate the prior and the likelihood. These combinations can take on both discrete and continuous forms. We also offer a variety of sharp subgaussian inequalities as a means of preparing for the analysis of convergence rates for Bayesian estimation. These inequalities involve a general and broad class of functionals known as negatively dependent binary random variables, which encompasses both the SCP and SRP settings. We investigate the relationship between these two settings and provide a concentration inequality for the empirical distribution of discrete random variables, which serves as a necessary condition for both SCP and SRP distributions. A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but we show that by modifying the state space, it is possible to tackle this problem using dynamic programming methods. Using empirical data on the level of incompatibility and real-world kidney transplant data, we create a comprehensive and realistic simulation, and through extensive computation, we find an optimal acceptance threshold for a sample set of patients. Interestingly, the findings suggest that accepting a kidney with a 4-antigen mismatch may not always result in a 50% lower transplant survival rate compared to accepting a 0-antigen mismatch kidney. This study provides an initial framework that can be improved with additional data, and highlights the importance of evaluating the level of incompatibility in decision-making, which has far-reaching implications not only for kidney transplants but also other organ transplants that face similar compatibility challenges. We propose several potential areas of expansion, such as incorporating uncertainties in the transition probabilities, developing a more sophisticated model of the level of incompatibility, and investigating alternative value-function approximation methods. We also provide a user-friendly summary of the research, along with a detailed numerical example, in the appendix. This work offers a valuable contribution to Transplantation Economics. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work offers a mathematical framework for understanding these models that complements the existing linguistic analysis, providing a quantitative exploration of the embedded structures and the corpus-generated distributions that they capture, as well as guidance on their application to time-series corpora. We also discuss the implications of these findings for various applications, including the analysis of company names, the construction of word2vec-based sentiment dictionaries, and the segmentation of financial texts. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/word-embeddings-in-finance. Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems. 
In both cases, the fair-throughput exceeds the SISO-OFDM counter part by 2.6bps/Hz, while the sum-throughput of MISO-OFDM outperforms the SISO-OFDM counterpart by 12.5bps/Hz. 
In both scenarios, additional gains of up to 25\% and 50\% can be achieved for moderate load conditions when comparing MISO-OFDM to SISO-OFDM, and MISO-OFDM to the upper bound, respectively. 
These findings are demonstrated using numerical data.

In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, the current state of the art requires an exponential number of rounds with an approximately $1/\sqrt{n}$-regret relative to the best rationalizable action when playing on a stationary distribution at round $n$. This study significantly improves that benchmark for general multiplayer games by $n^{3/5}$, achieving a polynomial-in-$n$ term when a non-uniform rationalizability condition is met. Notably, this breakthrough also yields a $n^{3/5}$-regret bound for best response against an unknown opponent in multiplayer games. Both of these results rely on a novel approach that combines the expansion-based algorithm with approximately efficient empirical risk minimization using a carefully designed weak learner, showcasing that this hybrid method is beneficial for solving various multiagent learning tasks. Lastly, this research provides a characterizing theorem for rationalizable behavior in multiagent learning settings. All of these findings are supported by a comprehensive set of numerical experiments presented herein. This study expands the set of multiagent learning problems it addresses, offering a new benchmark for future research. A high-level discussion of the $n^{3/5}$-regret bound obtained for the best shot problem in multiagent learning settings is also provided. A key aspect of this result is the fact that it is achieved with a non-uniform rationalizability condition. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread. These findings and their proofs are interesting because they show that the effects of complex dynamics in models that combine epidemiology and network theory are not always the same as their equivalent compartment-based models, and also provide insights into these dynamics that have not been seen before. These results are a significant step towards understanding these dynamics and could potentially apply to real-world situations, such as the spread of diseases on air travel networks. to any given history, which complicates multiple tasks including dialogue paraphrasing 
and summarization. To effectively tackle these challenges, our research introduces 
the MultiTalk Dataset, which is distinct from other large dialogue datasets like the 
ConvAI2 collection and the Emergent Dialogue Data. This new dataset comprises nine 
different text genres and our experiments reveal substantial diversity in responses 
along with notable amounts of generation noise. To further explore our findings, we 
created two distinct evaluation systems for ranking dialogue systems: one focused on 
paraphrasing and another on summarization tasks. Both of these systems were put to 
use on the newly introduced MultiTalk Dataset, which our research hypothesizes will 
be a valuable resource for testing and refining various dialogue systems including 
those generating concise summaries and paraphrased dialogue. With nine distinct text 
genres to choose from, this new dataset offers numerous possibilities for future 
research and analysis. Notably, our results reveal that simple approaches like the 
Markovian model are highly effective at capturing the diversity and complexity of the 
MultiTalk Dataset, which our research aims to make freely available for the public.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We show that these domains are each realization of a single, time-evolving imaginary surface, whose harmonic extension into the complex plane is determined by a single Gaussian free field combining the imaginary part of the upper half-plane and the imaginary part of the first orthant. This combined field exhibits rotationally invariant correlations, revealed through the statistics of line segments within the evolving domains. From this, we obtain specific probability measures encoding the time-evolving geometry of these domains. Notably, one-sided versions of the Airy2 and the Bessel2 processes emerge as local correlations, depending on the angle from which the domains are examined. On a larger scale, the domains exhibit self-similarity at any given length scale, with the measure of their boundary behaving like three times the length of the scale. This behavior is induced by the statistics of the underlying stochastic processes driving the SLE, which in turn influence the time-evolving imaginary surface and thus the domain's geometry. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the harmonic extension of the imaginary part of the first orthant exhibits rotationally invariant correlations, allowing for a two-parameter generalization of the model, where the statistics of the driving process on the positive reals can differ from that on the real line. This more expansive model yields a more complex, non-radially symmetric geometry of the domains, with different probability measures depending on the angle from which the domains are examined. This additional generality is demonstrated through numerical analysis of the stochastic processes' time series data from various statistical tests, confirming the reality of the described geometric phenomena. These findings emerge from an interdisciplinary approach that combines stochastic partial differential equations, statistical physics, and complex analysis with numerical analysis and statistical science. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additional analysis has been performed to evaluate the effects of cell type, tissue type and type of annotation on our results. Our comprehensive dataset on the results of one hundred plus tissues and cells types, combined with re-ranking analysis, is available at http://geneannotation.org/. Our research highlights the intricate relationship between the genomic environment and the effects of associated SNPs and provides insights on the limited influence of protein-coding regions. With an expanding scope of annotated data and better available computational power, our approach enables the comprehensive analysis of large association studies across numerous annotation types. Our work is particularly relevant for ongoing projects such as the NIH's Common Fund's Epigenome Roadmap Project and the ENCODE project. Our findings suggest that the majority of trait-associated SNPs target cell-type specific transcription factor binding sites rather than open or accessible regions and the limited influence of protein-coding regions on traits may be a result of their limited degree of expression and the specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits. Our results are compatible with the expression of most genes being unnecessary for the development of most traits and the potential of future projects like the ENCODE 2.0 project, that aim to comprehensively analyze the relationship between genomic regions and gene expression, in numerous cell types and tissues, to further understand the complex relationship between genomic environment and the effects of associated SNPs. Our approach enables the analysis of large association studies across numerous annotation types and our results, with their wide range of applications, are available at http://geneannotation.org/. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way that have been monitored over a decade or more have indicated that some seemingly persistent sources may actually be transient neutron star binaries in quiescence.  To account for observations of sources like AX J1845.9-0255 and 1RXH 16402-4893, which have luminosities well below their outburst levels and have not been observed during the known high-energy episodes of their counterparts, we propose a longer average period of $20\pm10$ years between these sources' outbursts.  This period is supported by historical data on radio and optical observations and would also explain the variable patterns of massive star formation that give rise to these binaries.  Furthermore, a statistical analysis of recurrence times for a larger sample of known LMXBs that contain neutron stars as companions places their average period at ~25 years, with a spread of about 10 years.  This average period of 25 years could also be inferred from the total observed duration of the 2004 outburst of GRS 18096, which ended about 15 years ago.  If this period holds true for the most deeply occulted sources like AX J1837.4-0248 and XTE J1835-425, which have not been observed during the past 15-20 years, it could account for the large numbers of transient X-ray binaries within the Milky Way.  With an average period of 25 years between outbursts, and considering that each source is only observable during its active period, it's likely that many of the variables in the Milky Way that have been monitored over a decade or more may actually be transient in nature, and that a significant population of neutron star binaries remains unaccounted for. This work's findings have significant implications for the development of more sophisticated, semantically diverse conversational agents. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived. Interestingly, the distribution of these sizes exhibits a power-law characteristics with a maximum cut-off point. This phenomenon is further illustrated through numerical analysis. Finally, the findings presented here offer a tangible platform for validating the predictions made by percolation theory and provide a meaningful context for extending the micro-level analysis to real-world networks. This approach may also contribute to the development of more precise and customizable destruction network models. This research was previously published in the journal arXiv. This is not our original work, but an extension of the ideas presented in arXiv. This extension includes additional numerical analysis and a new section titled "Network Destruction as an Information Flow". This new section explores the relationship between the destruction of networks and the flow of information within them. It also offers two contexts in which the micro-level approach may be applicable and provides a set of open research questions in this area. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. With current technological capabilities and materials, this design can be implemented on existing detectors with minimal modifications, offering a promising short-term solution to enhance the detectors' capabilities. A broader design space is also identified that can accommodate a wide range of coupled resonant systems, opening the way for innovative configurations that can tackle a wide range of challenges in gravitational wave detection. Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are subject to space-based disruptions and varying ranges that affect how data is perceived by nearby devices. With a high number of devices often present in applications for these systems and the scarcity of pilot signals available for them, designing protocols and scheduling algorithms is increasingly complex. To address this challenge, a new joint protocol has been developed that leverages varying reception areas of devices for better access and prioritizes the scheduling of devices with non-overlapping reception areas for maximum efficiency. According to the results obtained, this new scheme delivers considerable gains over traditional approaches, facilitating the simultaneous use of a large number of devices in MIMO arrays and enabling a more flexible design where the scale of the array is directly related to the size of the surrounding area. The code for this research can be found at https://github.com/ali-khonzani/XL-MIMO-RAP.

Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that the morphological structure of young stars' surrounding disks comprise various shapes, including symmetrical patterns and features resembling spiral arms, and localized curved formations. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Our model achieved the top score in the SwitchCam conversation generation challenge and displayed consistent improvement over traditional neural models in various evaluation metrics. With its capability to balance static $n$-gram bases and neural models, this model has significant practical value in real-world applications. The code for this model is available at https://github.com/THU-CLGRT/NgramRes.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach achieves simple and intuitive results, as demonstrated on challenging real-world images. The associated code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zwang615/SADRNet. The datasets used in this research are publicly accessible at https://www.tuebingen.datenteam.de/projects/3D_Florence. The 3D reconstruction and alignment visualizer developed in conjunction with SADRNet is available online at https://www.tuebingen.datenteam.de/projects/3D_Vis.

A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. This difficulty could, in turn, impact the effectiveness of pricing mechanisms and other grid management tools. This study provides a tangible, real-world example that utility companies, policymakers, and regulators can use when designing future grid management strategies. These strategies will need to account for the complex, often hard-to-predict aspects of storage units' behavior. This includes their reactions to risk and prices, which are crucial for maintaining a healthy, resilient power grid. This study on risk-averse storage units also raises broader theoretical questions about the risks associated with centralized authority and the potential benefits of decentralized systems that promote local innovation and decision-making. This is particularly evident in the context of energy management. This context presents a unique test case that can be applied to a wide range of complex systems and networks in various fields, including but not limited to transportation and finance. Satisfying the needs of various stakeholders, including but not limited to investors, end-users, and operation companies, is a key challenge in this context. This challenge can be addressed through a comprehensive risk management framework that prioritizes risk-aware storage units that take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This framework can be made up of multiple layers, each with its own set of risk management and scheduling objectives for different groups of stakeholders. This includes central authorities, storage units, and grid operation companies. This study also introduces three novel price speculation-based risk management approaches for central authorities, storage units, and grid operation companies. These approaches can be implemented at the local level to maintain the balance and stability of the power grid. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. This model incorporates a neutral edge state and resembles previous findings related to magnetic edge states in two-dimensional topological insulators. It also highlights unique features of HgTe, such as a considerable length scale where interaction between edge and bulk states exhibits resistance oscillations. This work delves into examination of the edge state's "winding number" or "topological charge" that governs resistance oscillations, examines the possibility of extending the concept of topological edge states to two dimensions, and emphasizes the unique advantages of HgTe in exploring these edge state phenomena over an extensive length scale. This is particularly evident in the behavior of small-sized samples. A theoretical analysis that incorporates interaction between edge and bulk states at the neutral point, along with discussion on the significance of "winding number" or "topological charge" and possible generalization to two-dimensional topological materials, has been included as part of the discussion. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, yet this flexibility also enables a global problem - interference. This research explores a new challenge it introduces - mixed-mode scheduling, where different cells transmit on different modes. A key difficulty arises as a result of TDD modes being treated as non-cooperative "prisoners' dilemma" games, where the optimal cell behavior maximizes overall throughput while causing internal conflicts. Moreover, the model's flexibility allows it to incorporate additional real-world variables, such as different cell transmit powers, by incorporating them into the "logistic" regression model as additional variables. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This finding fills a critical gap in previous high-energy nucleon-nucleon collision studies and provides a solid foundation for further analysis, such as studying collisions between heavy ions in high-energy experiments. The precise cross-sectional measurement also offers valuable insights for future experiments, such as those at higher energies with larger detectors. The observed top quark pairs had a mass range from 400 to 550 GeV, and the study focused on "prompt" jets that appeared within 4 nanoseconds of the collision event time, indicating that the quarks themselves rather than their decay products were responsible for the observed phenomenon. The findings have been made publicly available on the CMS website. The research was supported by funding from 2,500 institutions worldwide, and the resulting data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity became the basis for 17 individual papers on proton-lead collision research.
