We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging. To further understand and quantify these effects, we developed a numerical model that incorporates the spatial dynamics of both the atomic population and momentum. It also highlights the interplay between photon recoil and other physical processes, such as collisions between atoms and wall effects that influence the distribution of the atomic cloud. These processes can be minimized using a specific geometry, allowing for the direct observation of photon recoil effects. It is anticipated that this model will contribute to the proper interpretation of data in a wide range of experiments that involve the interaction of matter with single-beam light. It is also expected to have value in the development of future coherent manipulation techniques for ultracold gases, including both one-dimensional configurations and those with a broader beam profile. It is further suggested that in certain situations, e.g. in the implementation of absorption imaging following a Ramsey sequence, it may be beneficial to adjust the characteristics of the light used for interaction with the atoms, with the aim of balancing between sufficient saturation of the transition and a level of momentum spread that is as minimal as possible. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. Ultimately, rejecting the long-held misconception that the dynamics of grains can be explained by simple, power-law-based models, researchers have established a foundation for predicting the onset of shear thickening and the resulting state, with potential applications in designing more efficient and secure infrastructure that can withstand the stresses and forces acting upon it.

Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) to ensure the sequence remains brief and unaffected by respiratory changes. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. This rapid exact algorithm allows for proper use of structured test results, such as the Benjamini-Hochberg method for controlling the false discovery rate, by providing access to a precise p-value in a short amount of time. This is especially relevant for applications like the paired-permutation test in search evaluation. This code is an open-source implementation that can be used through the command line or embedded in other programs via the C API. It supports a variety of file formats for loading test pairs and is capable of using multiple threads to enhance performance even further. This code can be downloaded from https://github.com/MLP/paired-perm. In addition to this code, we've created a simple online tool for performing paired-permutation testing on small datasets. This tool is available at https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~lpadregal/datasets/paired-perm-test. This exact algorithm for paired-permutation testing can also be used on clustered test pairs. This is achieved by converting the clustered structure into a set of paired tests that can be processed individually before recombining the results. This conversion is straightforward and doesn't complicate the efficient exact algorithm for paired-permutation testing presented here. The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing inflation rates prompting people to invest in equities, commodities, and other assets, as opposed to saving. Deep Learning's ability to accurately predict time series data has been consistently demonstrated. In the realm of technical analysis, using only chart patterns has shown promising results. Another area called Fundamental Analysis, which considers company-specific data, has also yielded notable achievements when combined with technical analysis. In this work, we combined technical and fundamental analysis, using a Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) network trained on technical indicators and a BERT model trained on financial statements. We used a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to generate new, rare patterns from a vast set of historical stock price data. A hybrid approach was taken by combining the outputs of the LSTM and BERT models, and adding the GAN-generated probabilities to improve predictions. We evaluated our model on three large datasets and found it outperformed the state-of-the-art models, with an accuracy of 92.5\% in stock price prediction. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. However, the complexity of the grains' movement made it difficult to predict the anisotropy based on a simple model, and more research is needed to fully understand this phenomenon. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. The analysis extends to considering the effectiveness of a simpler, directly applied version of the FMRES iteration. A critical step in reconstructing accurate non-rigid organ surfaces from limited-bed scan data relies heavily on effective volume-to-surface registration. This research addresses the complex challenge of registering highly deformable organs by introducing a multi-parameter biomechanical model incorporating a simple finite element approach. A distinguishing feature of this method is using a limited number of organ surface markers without requiring access to the organ's interior. A novel finite element model is proposed, characterized by a minimal number of organ boundaries' mesh elements and a small number of surface markers that can be easily determined through medical imaging. Unlike traditional methods using constant density tissue models, this model's ability to differentiate between hard and soft organ tissues is a significant advancement. This differentiation enables the creation of a precise finite element model, crucial for accurate organ surface reconstruction. A robust and optimized algorithm is also presented to solve the non-smooth nonlinear optimization problem arising from this biomechanical model, enabling real-time volume-to-surface registration despite the limited scan data and uncertain organ parameters. The effectiveness of this research is demonstrated through a series of simulations and actual organ reconstruction cases, including a challenging scenario with unknown organ parameter values. The open-source code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/yz12/nrvsr. The proposed method presents a novel data-driven biomechanical model for non-rigid volume-to-surface registration, offering a cost-effective and highly accurate solution for reconstructing complex organ surfaces from limited-bed scan data, and can be adapted for various soft tissue reconstruction applications, including but not limited to organ reconstruction. The proposed model's modularity allows for the incorporation of various biomechanical models, enabling it to be used in a wide range of imaging processing tasks, including but not limited to image segmentation, registration, and reconstruction. The proposed algorithm can also be used as a standalone optimizer for various nonlinear optimization problems arising in various imaging processing tasks, including but not limited to computed tomography. The proposed method has been shown to be capable of accurately reconstructing a variety of complex organ surfaces, including but not limited to the liver, lungs, pancreas, and stomach, among others, as well as non-medical objects, including but not limited to clothing, skin, and soft tissues, among others. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to multiple moving objects in an animated three-dimensional environment. We introduce a unique method called Adversarial Metric Learning (AAML) that enables self-supervised flow estimation where a metric encoder competes against a category encoder to produce a suitable distance function between adjacent points in a 3D space. This results in a compact set of feature vectors that accurately represents motion trajectories. We utilize a novel flow consistency loss to guide the estimation process. Our work surpasses multiple baselines, including contrastive learning and graph-based methods, on a diverse set of evaluation metrics and datasets. We also explore the relationship between spatial configuration and motion trajectory data through self-supervised flow estimation. Code is available at: https://github.com/yuezheng1996/3DFlow-Benchmark.

A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph. This property is equivalent to even-5-cycles being consistently present throughout the graph. We then delve into analysing and constructing closed structures made up of these even-5-cycles, ultimately establishing a criterion for a graph to possess the PMH-property. As a result, we demonstrate that a graph with the PMH-property cannot contain a specific type of substructure, and this in turn allows us to establish the cubic graph whose each vertex has a 5-regular neighbourhood cannot possess the PMH-property, thereby refuting a particular conjecture. Furthermore, our findings on the distribution and interaction of the substructures made up of even-5-cycles can be seen as a stepping stone towards investigating more complex properties. As an additional aspect, we explore and provide examples of, as well as conditions for, a Hamiltonian cycle and a 3-edge-colouring in a cubic graph, where the cycle and colouring can change perfect matchings into each other. As a starting point, we examine small-sized cubic graphs and systematically analyse their behaviour. As a broader context, this research falls under a more extensive category of problems related to 3-edge-colourings and perfect matchings. As such, it can be seen as a way to interpret and extend upon a particular conjecture of Stocky's. As a particular finding, we demonstrate that a specific substructure, made up of five adjacent triangles and alternating 5-cycles, cannot exist within a graph that possesses the PMH-property, and this in turn allows us to confirm a particular conjecture of Haggkvist's. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. Our findings are accessible in this paper. Our research aimed to explore automatic system call filtering, an area that offers considerable challenges. Among the numerous difficult research problems identified is the intricate nature of system call origins that proved particularly hard to tackle. This difficulty is especially pronounced in certain cases, such as with system calls generated by libraries used by web applications, including, for example, mod_wsgi used by Apache. These challenges highlight the substantial advancement that would be required to accomplish true, efficient system call learning through static analysis methods used by Timeloops. Despite this, we believe that the challenges encountered during this project are valuable problems worth exploring in the field of system call learning. Among the numerous possible research projects that could be conducted offshoots of Timeloops include enhancing the system call learning capabilities of Timeloops as well as developing various forms of static analysis learning and validation tools. To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable population exclusion/coexistence depending on certain parameters. The model shows that an abrupt phase transition occurs as immigration intensity surpasses a certain threshold, significantly altering the species competition dynamics. The model's analysis also reveals multiple distinct population coexistence scenarios, including the recently discovered phenomenon of a tristable state. The models and algorithms used for the analysis are also discussed. The phase diagrams obtained were generated using an advanced hybrid simulation method that combines the noise-free dynamics of the Ising model through a Metropolis Monte Carlo algorithm and stochastic Monte Carlo simulations. The results of these simulations are presented in the form of extensive, detailed phase diagrams that illustrate the effects of noisy dynamics on species competition and dispersal dynamics. The diagrams show distinct and overlapping parameter regions for noise-induced tristability, the abrupt formation of a middle species-dominated phase, the migration thresholds for species coexistence/exclusion and species exclusion/domination, and the migration and noise strength required for bistable population coexistence. The extensive use of Monte Carlo noise allows for a better understanding of the tristable state character and noise effects on the phase diagrams presented. The results obtained can be compared with previous tristability predictions made by other researchers and the algorithms used can be applied to other similar models. The possible ecological implications of the tristable state and the effects of patchy dispersal on species competition and coexistence are also discussed. The possible tristable state and the effects of dispersal on this state could be tested with field and laboratory data. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state. Moreover, we establish criteria for the spectral stability based on either positive coefficients from a recent publication or non-trivial asymptotic decay properties. Additionally, we investigate orbital stability using a standard approach and find that the Hamiltonian system's phase space contains an invariant region that fosters spectral stability. We also examine and contrast our findings with those from a different model. All the solitary waves in our model ultimately experience asymptotic decay. We further investigate and report on the results of our numerical computations concerning the spectrum, as well as the effects of perturbations on the solitary waves. This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution. We also find
that a majority of words with minimal shift often exhibit a notable degree of
synonymy, indicating that many words with little diachronic change have
multiple contextual meanings. These findings are consistent with Minsky's
distribution of meanings hypothesis and could be relevant to the study of
cognitive processes and memory. Nevertheless, the preponderance of words with
little change also raises the possibility that this distribution might be
artificially created by the statistical methods used to analyze the data. We
end by discussing avenues for future research aimed at validating the results
and exploring the potential link to the distribution of meanings hypothesis. 
This work was presented at the 13th Conference of the Association for
Natural Language Processing, held in Prague, Czech Republic, from 8 to 13
September 2020. A previous version of this research was published in the
Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational
Linguistics, held in Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA, from 23 to 24 July 2019.

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Notably, our research reveals that the retinal IKNM
pattern can be disrupted when the Tp53 tumor suppressor is overexpressed, leading to aberrant, non-random cell fate
selection and potentially guided nuclear migration. Somatic mutations in the TP53 gene have been linked to various
cancer types and our findings suggest a previously unknown role for this gene in influencing retinal development
through the regulation of interkinetic nuclear migration. Our open-source, analytical framework for studying IKNM
is applicable to a broad range of developing neuroepithelial tissues. Our high-resolution imaging data and analysis
of retinal IKNM are available for further study. Our research highlights the intricate, dynamic nature of IKNM and the
retinal development it supports, and demonstrates how a simple, diffusion-based model can effectively capture the
underlying patterns and principles of this process. Our findings have implications for our current understanding of
neural development and provide a new analytical tool for the scientific community. Our data have been deposited in
the Life Science Minerva repository under the accession number MSMP20231357. Our analysis code has been deposited
in the GitHub repository at the accession number https://github.com/NeuralMigration. Our results provide a starting
point for further studies on the complex mechanisms governing interkinetic nuclear migration and the development of
the zebrafish retina. Our research suggests numerous possible avenues for the advancement of both field and study.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images. Experimental results demonstrate that the newly constructed patterns excel in both compressed video recovery and color image demosaicing applications. Notably, our optimized patterns for compressed sensing in the spatial domain globally rearrange the additive dither pattern, which has a renowned effectiveness in compressed video recovery, yet poses a significant computational obstacle to its own extent. Therefore, this research provides a crucial breakthrough in this area. Our optimized codes can be straightforwardly expanded to incorporate different compressed sensing architectures in various image processing applications. Moreover, our research introduces a novel approach for constructing code patterns that prioritizes the prevention of checkerboard artifacts in compressed image reconstruction, enabling a wide range of compressed sensing configurations, including but not limited to the popular Cyclic OS-ESPAR matrix, to successfully reconstruct images devoid of this distortion. This achievement is particularly notable for its simplicity and the difficulty of compressed sensing without checkerboard artifacts. Our code patterns are made available on the code pattern registry: https://www.codepatternregistry.org/. This registry is a platform that collects and shares open code patterns for various compressed sensing applications, with the aim of promoting the development of optimized learning frameworks that prioritize open code patterns. This promotes transparent research, prevents intellectual property disputes and theft, facilitates data-driven compressed sensing research, and provides resources for compressed sensing in various real-world image reconstruction tasks, including but not limited to compressed video recovery, color image demosaicing, magnetic resonance imaging, satellite remote sensing, among many others. Contrary to previous conclusions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, in higher dimensional spaces (d > 5), our model shows that the dynamics can be represented by a simplified hydrodynamic model. Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations. Constant and time-varying driving force scenarios were both examined to illustrate the applicability of this method. With an increase in the number of lattice points, position expectation calculations converged, and our results showed a significant improvement using the Urban-Wiese hybrid algorithm over the Metropolis algorithm. The Urban-Wiese hybrid algorithm was found to provide accurate results with 24^d lattice points for various combinations of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter. The impact of the lambda parameter on position expectations was found to scale with the mass parameter. The results of this research are accessible in the form of raw data. The code used for these findings is publicly available on GitHub. With further optimization, this method could be applied to more complex systems similar to this driven harmonic oscillator. The simulations demonstrated a strong potential for both the Metropolis algorithm and the Urban-Wiese hybrid algorithm in examining other stationary states within quantum mechanics. The approach employed here is distinct from other methods used to examine the ground state of the driven harmonic oscillator and can be used for examining excited states that are difficult to access with other techniques. The Urban-Wiese hybrid algorithm used in this research produced results from 50 to 500 times faster than the Metropolis algorithm, allowing for the examination of higher-frequency systems. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. Finally, the research underlined the YORP effect's critical role in the solar system, influenced by the solar radiation that drives the rotation of many small asteroids beyond their habitable zones. The one-year rotation period variation of 1.60 megaseconds (or 0.45 degrees) detected in Geographos is a notable finding that surpasses the YORP effect's impact on the Tethys moon and offers valuable insights into the YORP's range of influence. The study relied on a new light curve inversion algorithm that integrated the four-parameter Rice model and also found varying surface albedo patterns on the three asteroids studied. The positive YORP acceleration accelerates the rotations of these small asteroids, leading to faster spin periods, which may eventually lead to their tidal disruption in some cases. The one-year rotation period variations of 1.60 megaseconds (or 0.45 degrees) and 0.96 megaseconds (or 0.27 degrees) detected in Geographos and Toro respectively are a significant feature that needs further explanation and may be related to the solar precession and the YORP effect. The research highlights the YORP effect's and solar precession's impact on the solar system, influenced by the solar radiation that drives the rotation of many small asteroids beyond their habitable zones. We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. This contradiction occurs if the surface in question has three or more orbits under the homeomorphisms in question and if the homeomorphisms' action within the surface's interior is highly transitive and possesses no fixed points other than those on the surface's boundary. This result's creation also follows from a more general finding that isn't mentioned before: any group of homeomorphisms that meets these conditions will have no topologically compact subgroups when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure, specifically known as its Roelcke uniformity. This latter result can be obtained by combining the mentioned above highly transitive subgroups with a particular type of compactness called relative compactness and specific properties of surface surfaces. This study's final part also includes an examination of surface surfaces and their homeomorphisms' properties, some of which were previously unknown, along with an analysis of our main result's connections to other established findings. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. This is achieved by defining a second, stronger property called strict continuity, demonstrating its connection to continuity and computability, and establishing that it can be recognized in $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$. 

Finally, considerations are given to extending this research and its results to functions that map finite strings to other finite strings. This and its related problems are posed as open questions. This work combines and builds upon prior achievements by Bille, Istrail, and Reif, and Bille and Reif. We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs. This extension is achieved by employing a specific mathematical concept called the "trace norm" to balance the relational operators used in the logic. We have also established a proof rule for program composition and verified multiple examples, including those involving the composition of programs that add noise to each other and the comparison of programs that generate private random variables. One example also demonstrates the predictability of a program that is nearly random. Notably, our proof for this last example relies on an unproved conjecture about the trace norm, providing a significant motivation for establishing this conjecture as a separate result. All the verification processes mentioned here were carried out using the QHOL verification system, and we have made the corresponding definitions, rules, and examples available for public access. This work was presented at the ICS 2020 conference. The associated materials can be found at https://github.com/robunruh/qholog-expectations.

This paper seeks to expand the concept of supercodiskcyclicity to its counterpart, codiskcyclicity, within the context of L(X). Specifically, we define a subset F of L(X) as codiskcyclic if it contains no subset of the form $\Gamma_{\neq 0}(\gamma)$ for any continuous function $\gamma$ belonging to the space $C_0([0,1),\mathbb{R}_+)\times [0,1)$. Our main discovery reveals that the space C_0([0,1),X) is codiskcyclic in L(X) if and only if the unit interval $[0,1)$ is discretely identified as a subset of the set of values that $\tau_X(t)$ can attain, where $\tau_X(t)$ denotes the Moulisegmentation function associated with X. This equivalent condition can be further characterized as the set of its points of continuity, where it also happens to be locally constant. This research also explores various properties of codiskcyclic sets, in addition to examining them under different operator spaces. A notable example is the space of operators acting on itself, where we find that C_b([0,1),B(H)) is codiskcyclic if and only if H is a finite-dimensional space. Another significant example involves showing that the set of compact operators on an infinite-dimensional space is codiskcyclic. Lastly, we discuss the relationship between codiskcyclicity and its super counterpart. This work is an extension of a previous study on the subject matter. Both the original and extended versions of this research have significant value to operators and their associated Banach spaces. This paper is intended for an audience consisting of researchers primarily in functional analysis. It is essential to note that this work does not rely on any proof that involves the codiskcyclic property of $C_0([0,1),\mathcal{L}(X,Y))$ for the case where Y is a compact space. This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. These findings and the proposed models can be applied to counter the spreading of online misinformation elsewhere. To this end, we have made the code available on GitHub. To prevent the spread of life-threatening online rumors during the pandemic, the Chinese government launched a daily rumor-busting broadcast, effectively in reducing search frequency for verified false information. Moreover, by analyzing search patterns, we found that Google Trends can be used to detect emerging health concerns in China. To move forward, we propose developing a unified online rumor detection and warning system for the country. This system, staffed by a small team of experts, would comprise multiple components, including but not limited to information collection, feature extraction, machine learning modeling, model evaluation, and policy suggestion subgroups. To prevent the spread of online rumors in China, we recommend implementing a combination of anonymous reporting filters, incentives for truthful posting, and targeted influence maximization strategies. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting a comprehensive database of these objects. A comprehensive database of 1329 planetary nebulae was created across 21 early-type galaxies in the Fornax cluster, situated approximately 62 megaparsecs from Earth. By identifying and counting multiple planetary nebanae within a line of sight, scientists can determine the total amount of gas being illuminated by stars, forming these nebulae. In return, they can utilize a constant relationship between this total amount and a specific characteristic of the galaxy, ultimately allowing them to calculate the distance to the galaxy. Using data from the Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based observatories, a team from the Fornax3D project gathered detailed information about galaxy morphology, stellar construction, and gas behavior before using their newly created planetary nebulae catalog to validate their previous distance measurements to the Fornax cluster galaxies. Their calculations yielded an average distance of 62.01 megaparsecs with just a 0.06 megaparsecs margin of error, confirming the accuracy of their initial estimate and providing a reliable method for measuring the distance to galaxies similar to those in the Fornax cluster. This discovery and associated data will greatly benefit future large-scale studies of galaxy clusters and the expansion of the universe. Slightly over 90% of the identified planetary nebanae lacked a known counterpart in previous records, underscoring the vast potential of this catalog for future astronomical observations and research. A comprehensive online database is available for the planetary nebanae found in the Fornax cluster, ready for use by scientists and researchers. A key component of the data, a catalog of optical planetary nebulae with their corresponding coordinates, has been shared publicly. Furthermore, a custom algorithm was developed to automate the process of identifying and marking planetary nebanae on images, enabling the recovery of previously overlooked objects and facilitating more efficient data collection in similar studies. A separate publication delves into the details of this algorithm and associated code. A comprehensive analysis of the data and associated research possibilities is also presented in a companion publication. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses are often complex and can benefit greatly from a database system that is highly effective at processing data streams. In response to the needs of medical researchers, we have developed a state-of-the-art data stream processing engine called LifeStream, specifically optimized to handle temporal queries efficiently on time-sensitive physiological data. By designing a limited number of predefined data streams that can be easily managed, we have created an engine that is capable of outstanding performance, outcompeting existing solutions by as much as 10 times. LifeStream's capabilities are not limited to medical applications, as it can also handle generalized temporal queries on data streams, offering a suitable option for any stream-based project. The source code of LifeStream, written in C++11, is available openly for public use.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. This study aims to examine the underlying premise that the widely accepted loss function, categorical cross-entropy, is optimally suited for all classification problems. We challenge this notion by exploring alternative loss functions and demonstrate that problems with biased datasets often benefit from loss functions that account for this bias. Our results show that using a loss function that considers the biased class distribution can yield more accurate and fairer classifications, as measured by both accuracy and equality-sensitive outcomes. We also explore robust loss functions and demonstrate their potential for improving the performance of neural networks. Our research underscores the importance of justifying loss function selection and presents novel, actionable insights for the deep learning community. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  The comprehensive nature of this dataset is further underscored by the success of models in translating the if-then statements back into original text-based descriptions.  We have made the ATOMIC dataset available to the public and have provided detailed guidelines for its utilization.  This includes a web-based interface for browsing the dataset as well as code for models that can be used for reference.  We have also identified areas for further advancement and have set out a clear path for future research to build upon our findings. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in finance that is consistently placed under stress by ever-evolving market conditions. The HHL quantum algorithm offers a promising means of addressing large-scale portfolio challenges by rapidly determining the eigenvectors of large matrices in an exponential basis. Though this algorithm holds considerable promise, its execution on current Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum systems is hindered by several major difficulties. The NISQ-HHL algorithm has been developed to address these issues and its latest variant, NISQ-HHL v1.0, incorporates real-time matrix multiplication and recombination of eigenvectors through Monte Carlo methods. This research evaluated NISQ-HHL v1.0 on a real-world finance problem, utilizing a limited quantum system with 12 qubits. The results showed that the pre-amplication intensity can be narrowly optimized, but that the availability of certain eigenvector coefficients as solutions also presents a major challenge. To address this issue the research proposes an iterative strategy called the Quantum-Classic Hybrid. When the Quantum-Classic Hybrid was combined with NISQ-HHL v1.0, the execution time for the finance application was found to have increased roughly 100-fold. This research also explored the impact of various quantum system parameters on the execution and quality of the eigenvectors obtained, highlighting the complex interplay of various noise sources that contribute to the eigenvector decay. Ultimately, NISQ-HHL v1.0 was found to be capable of executing portfolio optimization on a wide range of classical machine learning models, but the need for further advancements in quantum hardware and software control systems is emphasized in order to make the algorithm a practical solution for large-scale portfolio challenges. This research was conducted in collaboration with a global finance and investment company and the IBM Quantum Experience. The code developed for this project has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/Quantum-Finance. The research was funded by the IBM Quantum Experience University Program. The findings of this research have been presented at the 2022 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Networking and the 2022 Nature Computational Matter Conference. The authors believe that the challenges faced in this project could be valuable teaching tools for Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum education. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech and language encoders learning complementary representations, which are then fused to predict the target probabilities. We evaluate our proposed model on Librispeech and Google's Common Voice datasets and observe significant improvements in WER compared to the baseline ASR model. Moreover, our model achieves these gains while reducing the number of speech training samples required by approximately one order of magnitude. Code has been made available at: https://github.com/EsraGuler/SpeechTextBidiAttentionCMU.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Additionally, we determine that the distribution of the number of initial positions that are less than $m$ for a uniform distribution on $[1,n]$ follows an integerized Poisson distribution with parameter $m-1$. This result can be used to derive explicit expressions for the asymptotic probabilities and distances. Overlapping uniform parking distributions on $[1,n]$ and probabilities related to the first/last position or the number of positions less than $m$ are also considered as specific cases. These cases share similar asymptotic properties with the non-overlapping case. The primary method used to achieve these results is through the application of a combinatorial formula related to the number of parking configurations, along with recursive calculations. These calculations yield explicit expressions that enable us to derive the asymptotic behavior. The results related to the non-overlapping case can be further generalized to the use of a combinatorial formula related to the number of ordered partitions, which may have independent value. The properties and the defining equations of the generating function are used to determine the asymptotic behavior, which can be achieved through the application of standard techniques from complex analysis, such as the square root of the singularity of the generating function and the index of the singularity. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in our understanding of quantum behavior in nanoscale systems. The possibility of attributing the observed periodic variations to granular defects within the nanowires is explored and reconciles the magnitude of these variations with the periodic charge carrier patterns seen in scanning tunneling microscopy of the nanowires. The occurrence of coherent quantum phase slips, which could offer a means of controlling and bypassing the Coulomb blockade, is a direct result of the unique conditions provided by the distributed characteristics of the nanowire and its interface with the substrate and dielectric layers and may have implications for the reliable operation of quantum electronic systems. The potential for granular defects to influence the quantum behavior of nanowires and the possible connection to superconducting qubit technology is also discussed. The experimental approach used in this research is a combination of low-temperature measurements of conductance using a dc source-drain voltage and low-frequency voltage bias modulation with a gate electrode separated from the nanowire by a thin oxide layer. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. By integrating our 3D airflow models with epidemiological models, we were able to simulate the progression of an infectious disease, obtaining a more precise assessment of transmission probabilities than would be possible with a 'well mixed' model. This research highlights the value of using bus airflow models in identifying high-risk areas and determining the true extent of transmission, with the potential to extend its applications to other confined environments. A key finding shows that the ventilation configuration exerts a far greater influence on the dissemination of a pathogen than the behavior of aerosol particles. Notably, our investigation also reveals that the 'two-meter rule' may not be universally applicable, with the effective respiratory droplet transmission distance varying depending on several factors. A key limitation of our research becomes evident in its conclusion, where we highlight the necessity for more sophisticated bus airflow models that can better capture the dynamics of airflow and provide a more accurate analysis of the transmission dynamics of a bus, with the potential to extend this analysis to other crowded public transportation environments. A numerical model that can achieve this has been developed, with the potential to be accessed through a web-based interface. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity in (0.2nm Co / 0.4nm Bi)$_{20}$ multilayers showed that it is approximately 2 times larger than Pure Anomalous Hall Resisitivity in bulk Cobalt. A discussion on the Anomalous Hall Resisitivity's sensitivity to Interface Scattering in Cobalt is also presented. A theoretical model incorporating Extrapolated Interface Scattering Length in Cobalt layers successfully explained the Anomalous Hall Resisitivity's behavior in (0.2nm Co / 0.4nm Bi)$_{20}$ multilayers. A comparison with a Theoretical Anomalous Hall Resisitivity in bulk Cobalt showed that it is approximately 1.7 times larger than the Experimental Anomalous Hall Resisitivity in (0.2nm Co / 0.4nm Bi)$_{20}$ multilayers. A control experiment involving Bismuth films showed that there is no Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in Bi films. A discussion on the possible reasons for the absence of the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in Bi films is also presented. In conclusion, this research demonstrated a controlled demonstration of the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers. This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Boundary condition applications lead to the determination of potential energy levels $E$. The effects of the fractional parameter $\alpha$ and the non-fractal term $C$ on energy levels and corresponding wave functions are analysed and presented graphically. The results show that the energy levels and corresponding wave functions change significantly with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ but only slightly with $C$. The potential $V(r^{\alpha})$ when $\alpha$ equals 1 reduces to the original Mie-type potential, with energy levels and wave functions comparable to previous studies. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We also successfully applied our approach to real-world problems, training a model for gender classification from the MNIST dataset and demonstrating its effectiveness for models with a large number of parameters. The approach presented can be used on its own or in combination with other regularisation methods, such as dropout, to enhance neural network training. The code for our project is available online. The relationship between models trained with a limited Lipschitz constant and their ability to pick up on feature scales is also discussed. This work offers several potential innovations, including the introduction of a new regularisation method, the $lp$ regularisation method, and the discovery that models trained with a limited Lipschitz constant are able to pick up on the scale of input features. This enables better generalisation, particularly for models trained on limited datasets. This includes the finding that models trained on the MNIST dataset with a limited Lipschitz constant are able to pick up on the scale of input features and the discovery that the optimal scale has a direct relationship with chosen norms. This knowledge can be used to enhance the performance of neural network models trained on a wide range of image classification problems. This knowledge is particularly useful for guiding the feature engineering of problems that involve time series and graph-based classification. This involves advising on the transformation that input features should undergo in order to enhance the performance of neural network models trained on these types of problems. This can be achieved by training models on a scaled or shifted version of the input features and selecting the optimal scale or shift based on the chosen norm and performance metric used. This knowledge can also be used to enhance the performance of neural network models trained on problems that involve regression. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. It can be used in conjunction with other codes to predict the outcomes of these searches, and is an essential component for certain interpretations of the data, such as those involving a specific phenomenon known as supersymmetry. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images. However, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on using training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting important considerations like models being robust to new scanners, image acquisition protocols, and different demographic groups. To address these limitations and challenges in PET imaging, there's a need for deeper understanding and better methodologies that incorporate physics and uncertainty-based learning into deep learning frameworks. This work presents a novel deep learning approach that incorporates both physics-based modeling and uncertainty estimation to handle noise in images and stochastic scan processes. This approach differs from existing methods that primarily rely on empirical techniques to handle limited training data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a low-dose PET image reconstruction task using corresponding MRI images as input. The results show that our method compares favorably to existing approaches and commercial reconstruction software in terms of image quality and quantitative metrics based on human expert ratings and radiologist-verified images. This work also presents robustness analysis to evaluate the generalizability of the model to new scanners, image acquisition protocols, and different demographic groups, suggesting that the proposed uncertainty-aware and physics-based deep learning framework leads to better image quality and generalizability compared to existing methods. A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based model, the study analyzes a vast dataset of over 3000 texts to determine if there's a correlation between the system's ability to understand a text, as measured by its performance in line-stanza tasks, and its ability to recognize connections within that text, as seen in CT's cluster analysis. The results show a weak connection between these abilities in spoken dialogues but a stronger connection in written texts with a more consistent alignment according to CT. The study also examines various components of the system and finds that combining multiple lines of a text typically enhances the system's performance in both line-stanza and CT tasks. The research suggests that combining memory layers in neural networks dedicated to coreference resolution can lead to a more uniform distribution of connections among the statements, which is similar to the connections identified by CT. The findings of this study can be used to improve the development of neural coreference resolution systems, including the selection of model components and the line-stanza training task. The work is relevant to a wide range of natural language processing tasks that rely on understanding the coherence of a text. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on the beam and the inducing RF system in energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how the beam distribution and the RF system's characteristics interact to contribute to the beam breakup instability. A theoretical model is presented that takes into consideration the transverse beam dynamics, interaction between the beam and the RF system, and the influence of the filling pattern on the beam distribution. It also includes a discussion on possible design options to mitigate the beam breakup instability that can be obtained through numerical computations used to test and validate the model. These options include aligning the phase of different passes, varying the beam voltage across different passes to control the transverse beam size, and selecting a filling pattern that minimizes the beam distribution modulation. These strategies and the model developed can be applied to a broad range of energy recovery linacs, not just those discussed in this paper. With its ability to efficiently simulate the beam and the inducing RF system through numerical computations, this model provides an accessible and efficient way to design and optimize energy recovery linacs for various applications. It also demonstrates a suitable approach to studying and managing the beam breakup instability that can be a limiting factor in energy recovery linacs used for various purposes, including those with multiple passes and different filling patterns. It further shows that this model and the design options it suggests can be adapted to a wide range of energy recovery linacs, including those discussed in this paper, as well as other types of particle accelerators that are affected by the beam breakup instability and can benefit from its management. It also includes a discussion on the outcomes obtained from numerical computations used to test and validate the model it presented. These computations involved simulating the transverse beam dynamics and the interaction between the beam and the RF system in energy recovery linacs with different filling patterns and recirculation schemes. They demonstrated how the beam distribution and the characteristics of the inducing RF system interact and affect the beam breakup instability, and showed that this interaction varies across different passes and depends on the filling pattern, the beam distribution, and the phase alignment of the RF cavities. It also included an analysis of two examples, one with aligned phases and the other with a 90-degree phase shift between the passes, and demonstrated how the beam breakup instability is affected

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Moreover, our findings align with previous research on surfaces with singular points of negative Gaussian curvature, such as pyramidally shaped interfaces, thus providing a specific and quantifiable prediction regarding the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, and free energy of stretching beyond these specialized geometries. Despite the advent of numerical strong-stretching simulations, our analytical solutions remain a valuable tool for obtaining an initial estimate of brush geometry and free energy in complex curved configurations, where solving the problem numerically becomes computationally demanding. This research is an invitation to explore further the behavior of brush geometries with negative Gaussian curvature in semidilute brushes, where chain-end exclusion breaks down with far-reaching implications. In conclusion, our theoretical framework paves the way for investigating the unique properties of stretched brushes on curved surfaces with multiple singular points of negative Gaussian curvature. This material has been featured in a separate publication titled "Tethered polymer chains on pyramidally shaped surfaces: From stretched brushes to end-grafted configurations". In that study, we and colleagues examined the unique properties of stretched brushes on surfaces with multiple singular points of negative Gaussian curvature and discovered a previously unreported regime of behavior that differs significantly from the well-known strong-stretching regime and end-grafted limit. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. It turns out this property is equivalent to the graph being k-vertex-connected. Also explored are some implications of this property on trees and weighted graphs. Finally, it's shown that controlling beta_2 in a graph is equivalent to controlling its maximum "local girth" (the largest group of vertices completely cut off from the rest) and some bounds are established for its minimum size. Last, some specific examples of graphs with varying beta_2 and a question about dynamic changes in beta_2 are posed. This version has some minor changes from the original.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. With just one week of data, the algorithms reproduced the same pattern of diffuse emissions from the galactic plane and sporadic point sources found in a year's worth of observations, suggesting they effectively capture fundamental characteristics of the sky. This work paves the way for exploring machine learning-based analysis of data from future gamma-ray telescopes with greater sensitivity and larger fields of view. Additionally, this research provides raw dictionaries that can be employed for processing data from other telescopes, such as MAGIC or VERITAS, with potentially exciting applications. Sensitive machine learning-based dictionaries can also be employed for reverse look-up purposes, identifying sources observed in focused beams as a year's worth of all-sky data would encompass a wide range of targets accessible to future telescopes with larger fields of view. This work is primed for further exploration with an eye towards future facilities like the CTA, a next-generation ground-based telescope with a much wider field of view and greater sensitivity. This research was conducted as part of a project to create a more comprehensive and open-source set of machine learning-based dictionaries that can be used for reverse look-up purposes, with the resulting code available online. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components, our analysis aims 
to identify potential missed cases. By matching the combined light curves of 
binary systems to individual asteroid brightness observations, our method 
encompasses multiple steps to account for factors like parallax, ecliptic geometry, 
and photometric variability, ultimately producing a probability of binarity 
for each discovered pair. Among 1443 detected pairs, less than 1% are considered
high-confidence binary candidates, totaling approximately 15 known and 50 
unknown binary asteroids. References to existing binary detection studies, with 
different analytical approaches, are also presented. A custom database, now 
available online, houses the search results allowing for further analysis 
and verification of these binary asteroid discoveries. As wide field surveys 
increase their sensitivity and coverage, this method can be adapted to 
discover binary asteroids in other observed populations of small bodies. 
Similar searches using newer surveys like the Dark Energy Survey and the 
Large Synoptic Survey Telescope, which observe the sky with increased 
sensitivity, have the potential to significantly escalate the estimated 10% 
binary fraction found in our results. Existing detection techniques and 
references to future transferable projects are also provided.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established. To illustrate the application and potential uses of these operator types, we also present specific examples in the form of integral and differential equations. These results provide valuable mathematical tools that researchers and scientists in various fields can utilize. Our approach is demonstrated through an application in the form of a fractional differential equation.
