We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Our findings demonstrate that this approach yields a Dungeon Master capable of guiding players toward intents that it has not directly observed. With the incorporation of a theory-of-mind, our results also demonstrate that integrated intentions and contextual knowledge facilitate complex world-based goal attainment. Lastly, our analysis shows that a Dungeon Master's ability to assess the validity of its own intentions is directly correlated with its capacity to adhere to established game rules. All supporting data can be found at https://github.com/nytimes/s4c challenges.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. Notably, DISCO's capabilities extend to producing counterfactual data for multiple perturbation types without incurring significant development costs, setting it apart from comparable baselines. We have made the code and data for this project available openly.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. If successfully harnessed, this process has the potential to broadly expand the range of compatible substrates and reduce material waste.

However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any information regarding the irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  The paper also introduces a simple yet effective method for enhancing the conditioning of the generator.  All the developed techniques have been thoroughly evaluated and their impact analyzed in specific applications such as multi-label data generation and anomaly detection. The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing that the primary obstacle is the overwhelming low-energy radiation.  A key prediction of this research is the expectation of visible neutrinos in the telescopes for high sensitivity, corresponding to a detection of about 10-30 times the number of findings from the IceCube.  This could be influenced by the galaxies and their environments and may require a new generation of more powerful observatories to identify.  In essence, explaining the gamma-rays in the energy band of the 15 analyzed galaxies as a result of the MAD model would necessitate a much higher rate at which matter falls into the black holes.  Alternative explanations for these galaxies include the presence of pulsars, or a more limited range in energy band coverage.  With upgrades in sensitivity and coverage, future gamma-ray and neutrino telescopes will be able to better understand this phenomenon and provide new insights.  This research was conducted in partnership with the ANTARES, MAGIC, and VERITAS collaborations. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/Cheng-Zhang/FedHealth.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations. Furthermore, this study delves into the Stewart skewness optimization technique, alternative formulations, and the application of global optimization algorithms. Additionally, we discuss the kurtosis tax and counter-tax theorems, as well as some notable extensions and modifications. Some of these extensions include constraints on portfolio turnover, the number of stocks, and regime-switching models. This study also sketches some of the boundaries between and within various methodologies, with some numerical examples presented to illustrate the results and outcomes. With its comprehensive overview of higher moments portfolio optimization strategies and research, this study is set to guide Hedge Fund Industry practitioners and provide a platform for further research in this area.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach to selection is crucial. This process comprises multiple, interconnected problems, each mirroring a well-known computational issue. While individual research has been extensively conducted, an integrated examination of these problems is uncommon. This paper addresses two critical aspects of application processing: creating review and interview panels and scheduling interviews. We developed a prototype system to automate interview planning for a real-world scenario. Compared to existing, manual methods, our approach yields a superior plan. To achieve this, we evaluated different algorithmic options and tailored them to solve panel creation and scheduling issues. We experimented with these solutions using real data, presenting our findings. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. This study highlights specific examples of this type of mistake and offers suggestions for both modelers and researchers using existing models, including the incorporation of temporal dynamics and critical assessment of model assumptions through biologic and epidemiologic means. Ultimately, we stress that any model, once developed, requires a critical examination of its own, in addition to external validation, to ensure its accuracy and to prevent the fitting of noise rather than underlying patterns. This study is not a review of the current epidemic situation but rather a guide for modelers, public health officials, and all those interpreting and using mathematical models, and it is intended to contribute constructively to the ongoing discussion and efforts to control and manage the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to address issues of bias, fairness, and efficiency by incorporating causal knowledge into deep learning models. This field draws upon the foundations of machine learning, statistics, and causal analysis to build more accurate and effective models. A key differentiator of causal deep learning is its consideration of abstract concepts such as causality, effect, and counterfactuals through the incorporation of causal representations and learning objectives. As a result, there is a growing body of research characterized by diverse methods, models, and theories. This paper seeks to explore the diverse landscape of causal deep learning by categorizing methods along three dimensions: representation, prediction, and theory-based learning; providing an analysis of the relationships between reinforcement learning, causality, and learning dynamics; and highlighting prominent research, model architectures, and theoretical developments. With this work, we aim to contribute a comprehensive and structured understanding of the field, its many facets, and its numerous contributions, ultimately facilitating further advancement in causal deep learning.

By modeling the mechanical properties of heart tissue as three-dimensional layers, researchers have created finite element representations of the heart. Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized models such as Laplace diffusion, Coulomb diffusion, and their variants. Our results are derived through a combination of mathematical proofs and numerical simulations using a diverse set of scenarios. Our approach provides a practical solution for inferring diffusion characteristics from observed spatial distributions, missing from the existing literature. Our research also yields relevant mathematical expressions that are valuable to the broader scientific community. Our work is relevant to a diverse range of studies involving random movements, fluid dynamics, finance, and biology. Notable examples include the movement of the Ebola virus within the human body, the diffusion of contaminants in river traffic, the behavior of investors in financial markets, and the migration of cancer cells within tumorous tissues. Our results yield relevant mathematical expressions that are valuable to the broader scientific community. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Finally, we discuss and differentiate our approach from existing methods and theories in the field. It highlights the distinguishing characteristics of these spaces and their compactifications within the broader context of number theory. Key topics include a brief introduction to modular forms, the properties of spaces of modular forms, their analytic and algebraic compactifications, and an overview of related arithmetic invariants that can be found within these compactifications. It also addresses the fundamental difference between the Grassmannian Gr_{d,4} and Deligne's complex algebraic surface |M_d| that parameterizes d-fold covers of the projective line, specifically focusing on the relationship between these spaces and the Bass-Herrring-Mumford surface of degree 4d. It concludes by examining the Bass-Herring-Mumford surface and its connection to the number 24. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the observed flattening of the main sequence at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened shape of the main sequence at the high mass end. This study's unique approach and findings offer a distinct perspective on the main sequence, one that emphasizes the critical role bulges play in galaxy evolution. Certainly, the growth of bulges and resulting impact on star formation also suggests that many of these massive galaxies may have completed their significant star formation and are now evolving into older, more quiescent forms, with many possessing the characteristics of bulge-dominated galaxies like elliptical galaxies. The extensive database used in this study, along with its findings, are particularly valuable for guiding future research, such as large-scale observational projects like the DESI survey, which will obtain similar data but on much larger scales. This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, pre-trained
on three languages: English, Slovene, and Croatian. The paper investigates
various setups utilizing datasets from two languages and presents a straightforward
multi-task model to accomplish sentiment classification. The assessment involves
zero-shot and few-shot learning approaches within single-task and multi-task
experiments for both Slovene and Croatian. The findings demonstrate that the
zero-shot learning approach among the Slovene datasets yields comparable
results. However, the zero-shot learning between Slovene and Croatian datasets
achieves lower accuracy compared to few-shot learning. The research also discovers
that removing the classification head from the model before utilizing it for zero-
shot learning can boost the effectiveness by approximately 10%. The underlying
reason appears to be the head's limited knowledge of the model, which can be
illustrated using an attention heatmap. The research indicates that, when using
zero-shot learning among the Slovene datasets, the model prioritizes English
over Slovene, whereas when using zero-shot learning between Slovene and Croatian
datasets, the model favors Slovene over Croatian. The paper suggests several
possible explanations, including the head's bias towards the most extensively
represented language and the influence of the model's bias towards the most
numerous training samples. The research also explores the head's impact on the
zero-shot learning results by introducing a new approach called the zero-shot
tuning, which circumvents this issue. The findings demonstrate that, when using

the negative sentiment from the Slovene dataset due to the excessive amount of
data designating news articles as negative. The paper proposes several possible
exolutions, including oversampling the positive classes, employing a class-weight

However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets of any size by utilizing gradient-classified samples in close proximity to the decision boundary. To evaluate the proposed method, a concise dataset is utilized consisting of 188 COVID-19 x-ray images with corresponding text-based severity labels and ICU admission information. Key features are extracted from this compact dataset which is then used to train machine learning models for ICU prediction tasks. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, feature extraction methods are compared and machine learning models trained on these features to achieve ICU prediction accuracy results. The proposed approach and method for evaluating the hypothesis both take up relatively small amounts of space in comparison to existing research. The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory. This statement can be found in the work of Cigarri and Grandis, who attributed it to the late mathematician Charles W. Curtis. A distinct and independent proof of this result is provided here. Additionally, this proof's approach will be expanded to demonstrate that the universal simplicial group bundle W arises from a true group structure when the base simplicial set in simplicial groups over C is univalent groups. This particular conclusion has not been previously demonstrated in the literature. All previous results related to the universal simplicial group bundle holding for the category of strict monoidal simplicial groups in C or yielding a group structure when based on univalent groups also hold due to this proof's nature. These findings originated from the researcher's study of the work on univalent algebraic structures by Joyal and Tierney. A brief discussion on categorically describing the group structure and its relation to the simplicial Yoneda embedding is included. This proof utilizes a method it terms "simplicial unitary descent" which can be applied to lawfully defined simplicial universals. A more expansive analysis of this method and its consequences for simplicial universals, particularly including the standard simplicial universe, is presented in the paper's final section. A related preprint containing the proof is available online. This paper's results were announced in a 2022 abstract posted on arXiv. A more detailed examination of the simplicial group structure and its Yoneda relation is included in a 2022 technical report also available online. A prior related statement demonstrating that the universal simplicial group bundle arises from a group structure when based on univalent groups has been confirmed as new in a 2022 email conversation with the mathematician Joseph Shabunis. A distinct and independent proof of this particular statement is provided in the paper. A discussion on the relation between this proof and an alternative approach based on the monadicity theorem of Makkai and Paré in 1979 is included in the paper's section 4.3. A related issue with delooping laws, specifically categorically defined as right fibration laws, is examined in the paper's section

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), addresses this imbalance by incorporating a proposal-based class balance technique. This approach yields a more uniform proposal distribution, allowing our model to effectively learn from both simple and complex proposals. Our results show that with a proposal-based balanced sampling technique, our model achieves a notable 10.5% absolute improvement in AP on the Visual Relationship Detection V1.6 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art literature. Code is available at https://github.com/zwang-cse/SABRA-VRD.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from anisotropic accretion of gas, is responsible for their diminished star-formation activity in the disks while contributing to bulge construction in their centers. This is consistent with observations of some galaxies even in the distant past. Notably, one galaxy with an exceptionally developed bulge is present, to which this model could also apply. If our findings are confirmed, they could reveal that the anisotropic accretion of gas, building bulges and warping disks in the distant past, has been misconstrued due to limited-line-of-sight observation of some galaxies even at $\rm z\approx 3$. Moreover, this could result in an underestimation of the bulge construction rate in some quiescent, lopsided galaxies at this era. Both of these effects have notable implications for our understanding of the development of massive, quiescent galaxies and their ultimate transformation into bulge-dominated galaxies. Extremely irregular disk systems, which are resistant to quenching, also have the potential for being discovered in the present. Systematic observational efforts are required to either validate or refute our findings based on the analysis of multiple galaxy cores at $\rm z\approx 3$ and their corresponding member galaxies at $\rm z\approx 0$ and $\rm z\approx 2$. If our hypothesis is correct, then a focused study on some specific galaxy groups at $\rm z\approx 3$ with irregularly shaped disk systems at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems could yield a bulge construction rate in excess of $50\%$ and provide novel insights into the development of massive, quiescent galaxies and the mass distribution of gas and stars within them. Notably, this could also result in an overestimation of the star formation rate in some galaxies at this era. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence. Notably, satellite measurements at this event intensity have been scarce, giving this discovery considerable significance. Further examination of satellite data reveals that a previously overlooked signal from the solar flare's initial electron burst might hold crucial clues about this event. As a result of this new information, satellite and ground-based recordings of the event are being reinterpreted, offering valuable insights into solar flare genetics. This finding also paves the way for a revised solar flare classification system that could be reliably forecast from satellites. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster surface rotation rate compared to their core. We've identified a subgiant or early giant star, SPHINX-1, with a remarkably slow surface rotation rate of 0.46 nm/s, contrary to expected behavior. Analysis of SPHINX-1's internal structure suggests its core and outer layers are rotating at different speeds. There are a few possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation pattern, including the star experiencing mass loss that caused its rotation rate to slow or it ingesting a large planet that caused its rotation to speed up. Alternatively, this pattern could result from an unexpected treatment of angular momentum within models of this star or an overestimation of its mass. To confirm these findings, we suggest observing SPHINX-1 for stellar pulsations that could provide insights into this star's internal composition and rotation patterns. Additionally, we advise revising the parameters for detecting rotational splittings in the pulsation modes of similar stars that have retained their rapid rotation rates. This discovery and suggested modifications to its analysis can help our understanding of the behavior of rotating stars that have evolved into giants. This research was conducted using the PULPY code in conjunction with the PASTEL database. It shows that investigating the internal rotation patterns of giant stars can offer valuable information about their evolution and any anomalies they may have experienced. This research made use of the NumPy, SciPy, and matplotlib scientific Python packages as well as the Astropy library. This study also used the PULPY code developed by G. Houdek. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming, and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. This system has immense potential to be applicable in a wide range of applications involving unexpected events. This research also presents a new large multimedia dataset obtained from Weibo, specifically tailored for evaluating fake news detection models on the Chinese language. This new dataset, named WD-Dataset, is distinct from the existing datasets that primarily focus on text-based information and offers an opportunity to investigate the unique challenges faced by the current models in dealing with fake news on the Chinese language. This new dataset provides vital insights into the difficulties that the current models encounter when analyzing the false information on this language and the simple yet effective approach presented can be applied to enhance the performance of the current models. This approach involves the use of both absolute and relative absolute changes in the F1-score and accuracy metrics, offering a more comprehensive understanding of the models' performance, especially in the category-based evaluation, and providing a real-world perspective on the effectiveness of the models in detecting false information, as demonstrated on Twitter and Weibo. This research presents MetaFEND as a suitable baseline for the research community, presenting an open invitation to explore the various challenges and opportunities in this domain, and an opportunity to introduce a new large multimedia dataset obtained from Weibo, specifically tailored for evaluating fake news detection models on the Chinese language, named WD-Dataset. u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\mathcal{H}u(u_{x})+\delta u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.

Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\delta \geq 0$ and investigate the initial data that generates solutions with a singular behavior in a finite amount of time. Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. All previously known infinite sets of GCM quadruples in binary and quaternary spaces are enlarged to higher dimensions. A new approach for designing GCM quadruples is introduced and proven equivalent to an existing method. Further, an iterative procedure is described which can generate GCM pairs in any space and a method for translating two-dimensional GCMs to multi-dimensional spaces also known as matrix-complementary pairs. A brief discussion on the potential for constructing GCMs in spaces of five or more dimensions is provided. All the newly created GCM quadruples and pairs in this research are listed in the appendix. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-aperiodic valley interference patterns were directly visualized in silicon by employing scanning tunneling microscopy to investigate coupled atoms.
The examination reveals the significance of envelope anisotropy as it influences Heisenberg's spin exchange interactions that can be engineered atom by atom, thereby providing a precise and versatile approach to realizing quantum simulations and novel ferroelectric properties. 
The research demonstrates that precise placement of dopants in silicon is possible, offering a versatile framework for quantum simulations and solid-state physics that can be both experimentally controlled and theoretically analyzed. 
This control over the lattice-scale valley interference patterns, coupled with the capacity to manipulate spin exchange interactions, can enable innovative applications in quantum simulations, as well as novel ferroelectric properties induced by coupled donor arrays. 
In this context, silicon stands out as an exceptional material, complemented by advances in nanofabrication and cryogenic scanning tunneling microscopy that allow for the visualization and manipulation of quantum states at the atomic level. 
This breakthrough paves the way for exploring complex phenomena related to coupled donor arrays, and provides a foundation for discussing possible extensions, such as the inclusion of impurities in silicon-germanium and silicon-ribbons. 
In these systems, the valley interference patterns and spin exchange interactions can be influenced by interface engineering and edge effects, which can give rise to diverse and aperiodic patterns that can be both experimentally verified and theoretically analyzed. 
This then could potentially lead to innovative aperiodic patterns of the Xc (x-space) type, and may also enable the exploration of a wide range of quantum states, including aperiodic Kekule structures, valence bond crystals, and coupled Heisenberg chains, among others. 
In this sense, silicon's unique characteristics, coupled with the versatility of nanofabrication and cryogenic scanning tunneling microscopy, make it an ideal and accessible platform for quantum simulations and a wide range of solid-state physics research. 
This is because the donor arrays in this system can be designed to mimic complex many-body models that have a direct analogy with chemistry and physics, and can also incorporate edge and interface effects, as well as impurities

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. Notably, our approach and results remain relevant to a broad range of nonlinear dynamical systems that can be represented using the belief propagation algorithm. Our research was conducted in partnership with Google AI, and our findings are published in a paper that's available on arXiv. Existing studies primarily focused on linear systems' identification and analysis, without exploring the capabilities of graph neural networks. Nonlinear systems offer a rich area for investigation and can transport knowledge to a wider range of complex systems, not just linear ones. In our analysis, we extracted the intrinsic graph representation from a well-known nonlinear system – the Kuramoto network – but this resulted in a loss of nonlinear driving kernels. As a consequence, we were left with a linear system that could be easily analyzed, but it no longer possessed the characteristics of the original nonlinear system from which it was derived. Despite this constraint, our research demonstrated a promising capacity for transporting knowledge to a wider range of complex systems, including nonlinear ones. It's worth noting that the arXiv paper contains additional results not mentioned here, including the analysis of a nonlinear system – the Kuramoto network – and the discussion of its limitations. We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra. Our approach is characterized by utilizing a combination of combinatorial methods, algebraic tools from the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra, and applications of graded polynomial rings. As a result, we are able to generate recursive formulas for a range of parameters, offering a structured and systematic approach to analyzing the underlying patterns. This achievement is further illustrated by a representative formula derived from our method. Our methodology intentionally prioritizes explanatory clarity over computational efficiency in our recursive formulas, leaving room for possible optimizations. This work is closely related to a renowned result established by M. Snaith and refined by J. R. Wilson. This achievement is further extended to the homology of the stable orthogonal group by means of applying the Bockstein homomorphism. This work resulted in deriving a recursive formula for calculating the counts of the involved partitions, which can be utilized to explore the intrinsic properties of the stable orthogonal group. A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning-based methods have been successful in identifying this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Generator (PBLG) that combines two key concepts: progressive networks and generative adversarial techniques. The PBLG initially trains a basic encoder to recognize pre-LITT images, then gradually refines this encoder to mimic post-LITT images with different treatment stages. By leveraging both progressive and adversarial features, the PBLG effectively synthesizes a range of post-LITT images, enabling it to expand the limited set of training images available. Experimental results show that the proposed framework accurately generates diverse post-LITT images, even when given only a small set of pre-LITT training images. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph pattern matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted right regular sequence (RRS) as a faster alternative to pattern matching. Yet, developing a correct and efficient GP 2 program requires carefully constructing RRS sequences that not only substitute for pattern matching but also preserve program correctness. To facilitate easier GP 2 program development, we present a GP 2 compiler named improvedGP2, which complements the basic GP 2 type system and provides a more manageable way to define RRS sequences, thereby simplifying program verification and validation through type and value analysis. Additionally, we demonstrate the compiler's efficacy by applying it to a program from a previous experiment, showing it yields a 4.3 times improvement in execution speed. The improvedGP2 compiler is available online at https://improvedGP2.github.io/. For program verification and validation purposes, GP 2 programs can be downloaded from https://github.com/improvedGP2/examples. The underlying GP 2 framework and the extended environment are also provided for research purposes and can be accessed at https://github.com/improvedGP2/gp2. The improvedGP2 compiler uses Scala 3 and is compatible with Scala 2.13 and 3.0.x. To build the compiler, use the sbt build tool. To use the compiler, launch it from the command line as described in the usage section of the improvedGP2 website. The GP 2 framework comprises two main modules: the base framework and the environment, which can be installed separately on the target machine to speed up program analysis. The base framework has a footprint of approximately 340 MB on the JVM, whereas the full environment, including the compiler and development tools, occupies around 1.4 GB. Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, showcasing its versatility and efficiency in both unsupervised and supervised settings. The results obtained outperform the existing state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the framework's potential advantages. The framework's versatility also opens up possible applications in deep learning, including a two-stage unsupervised feature extraction technique called DeepCon. The code for the proposed methods and the numerical experiments is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/ChengZhiTang/Unified-Framework-for-Feature-Extraction. The code for DeepCon is also available at: https://github.com/ChengZhiTang/DeepCon. The results obtained can be improved further, presenting opportunities for future research. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs. Our approach involves a combination of techniques such as group theoretical properties, permutation group theory, and Ramsey theory to generate our infinite sequence of graphs. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. One potential application of this method is the enhancement of existing KBC models, as it can be used to pre-train models on an unrestricted knowledge base like Wikidata. One potential limitation of this approach becomes apparent during experiments, where the challenge of selecting appropriate knowledge graph entities to input into the model is identified. To address this issue, our work presents a straightforward yet effective method called Entity Disambiguation Network (EDN). One area where this approach may not offer significant improvements is in task types that are heavily reliant on local knowledge areas, such as CheM-30. To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously introduced by dividing lengthy sequences into multiple short chunks and processing them with a RNN based on the previous chunk. This model demonstrated superior performance in several metrics. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) is proposed to combine the dual-path RNN model with convolution recurrent units. In this model, each sub-path consists of a convolution recurrent unit and RNN, where the RNN uses the previous chunk as input. The DPCRN model utilizes 16-layer convolution recurrent units in each sub-path to process long sequences efficiently. The model is evaluated on the Librispeech corpus and demonstrates superior results over the dual-path RNN model, with a 3.4dB improvement in the wide band scenario and 3.5dB in the narrow band scenario. Additionally, it outperforms state-of-the-art models including Conv-TASNet and DenseSP, with only a 0.3 million parameters increase. Code is available at: https://github.com/ghr96/DPCRN.

A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux scheme's parametric controls while converging towards a fully explicit treatment. Yet, establishing trust in this innovative approach requires evidence that it can accurately replicate fundamental convection phenomena. This study employs a simple two-fluid single-column model to recreate a perfectally stable atmosphere subject to heating from below, resulting in the development of cellular convection patterns in the upper layers, as is commonly observed in Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard experiments and the atmosphere. We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. One such example involves replacing one of the JC-systems with a system that has pre-existing multipartite entanglement. Our study paves the way for exploring JC-interactions in multi-cavity setups, providing a means to generate multipartite entanglement from a highly entangled pair. Notably, this finding is particularly relevant for optimizing a recent experiment that successfully generated 24 individually measured JC-systems, and our predictions are compatible with its parameters. This work is also an invitation to re-explore an earlier proposal that suggested generating genuinely multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions in a 4-partite delta configuration. This can be achieved by placing two unconnected JC-systems at opposite ends of the delta, and it offers a straightforward method for creating large-scale genuine multipartite entanglement. This finding is a stepping stone for guiding future experimental and theoretical studies on, and implementations of, genuinely multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. This work is accompanied by numerical simulations that mirror the experimental setup of Ref.[34], along with an analytical discussion that includes a condition for inducing tripartite entanglement in a delta configuration. This condition is a necessary and sufficient requirement that is both a necessary and sufficient condition for inducing delta-entanglement. This condition is a delta-form of the necessary and sufficient condition for inducing bipartite entanglement in a cavity-cavity system, and it can be experimentally realized. This work offers numerical simulations that validate the analytical results, and it provides an invitation to re-explore the proposal of Ref.[25] that suggested generating a 4-partite delta-entangled state via JC-interactions. organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.

databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. A
document terrier search engine was used to retrieve relevant tweets based on pre-defined
search queries. We processed the tweets into a form that could be used by long short-term

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole that exists in a complex state of phase, known as the Yang-Yang critical state. By analyzing the non-linear EPYM gravity equations and employing numerical methods to solve them, we identify that there is a critical temperature associated with the phase transition that is directly influenced by the shadow radius. This relationship can be expressed through a set of nonlinear equations that we detail in this study. Non-linear effects play a substantial role in shadow geometry, and the relationship between temperature and the inner radius of the black hole creates a barrier that prevents the universe from entering a state known as the small-radius big rip in a gravitational system. This system is susceptible to non-linear interactions, as it allows for multiple phase transitions that are supported by the shadow radius. This finding can be applied to a broader non-Yang-Yang critical state, as it provides a mathematical expression that can be used to identify the phase transition temperatures for any given shadow radius. This expression can be further extended to a wide range of non-linear AdS black holes through a modified EPYM gravity framework, where it can be used to determine the phase structure and identify the non-linear electric charge, length, and temperature parameters that define these systems. This approach can be used as a foundation for analyzing and understanding the non-linear properties of black holes that exist in our universe. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Our findings show that observing these non-classical phenomena is as simple as looking for particular features in the tomogram, without the necessity for intricate quantum state analysis. This strategy is illustrated with a Schrödinger cat system that exhibits both non-Gaussian entanglement and synchronization, allowing us to visually identify these non-classical properties just by examining the structure of the optical tomogram. Our discovery offers a straightforward and efficient way of ascertaining the presence of these complex quantum properties, without the burden of full state reconstruction. This research is relevant for ongoing experiments in quantum optics and photonic systems, where optical tomography is employed to gather data, such as those with the AOs in the d-Shell atoms research, among others. This approach has the potential to be extended to the study of open quantum systems, offering a more accessible means of analyzing the intricate dynamics of many of today's photonic systems. This finding is also a significant demonstration of the benefits of combining theoretical analysis with experimental data, as is the case with the Munich group's EmDrive thruster experiment, where a pattern in the tomogram can indicate the onset of non-equilibrium quantum dynamics, without the need for full state reconstruction, further simplifying the data analysis to only looking at specific features of the optical tomogram, as is also shown in the research on the Michelson interferometer with moving mirror, among many others. 360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. Such data, particularly
found in 360-degree virtual tourism videos, can significantly steer user
attention toward certain parts of the video. Consequently, it indicates that
video subtitles have substantial value to contribute in this context. Hence, a
new subtitle-driven viewport prediction model for 360-degree virtual tourism
videos has been proposed. By integrating both the spatial information derived
from the video and the navigation hints present in the subtitles, the model
achieves a more accurate prediction of user views. Experimental results show that
the proposed model outperforms the current baseline methods of viewport
prediction based on head tracking and visual importance, respectively. The model
also demonstrates its own versatility in being applicable to various types
of 360-degree streaming videos. The underlying code of the proposed model is
made available on GitHub at https://github.com/{Author GitHub ID}/360VP.

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge when attempting to apply them to a broad range of temperatures, as most algorithms struggled with significant truncation errors when away from an extreme temperature regime. This issue hindered a major advantage of tensor networks - their local interpretation. To overcome this problem, a new class of tensor network architectures has been proposed that maintains the ability to accurately represent temperatures across a wide range of values. When applied to a specific temperature, these networks are able to locally adjust their site tensors to an exponential form, achieving a significant reduction in truncation errors. This novel approach can be combined with a range of existing time-evolution algorithms, allowing for a precise representation of time-evolved states in response to local environments over a broad temperature range. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we apply it to a widely recognized problem - the quenching of a Bose-Hubbard dimer from an highly correlated state. This research showcases that local site tensors with a genuine physical interpretation can be safely utilized in conjunction with a range of time-evolution algorithms, enabling a more all-encompassing understanding of both thermal states and time-evolution in complex situations. This approach can be applied to a diverse set of scenarios, including but not limited to, (1) two-dimensional Bose-Hubbard dimer under quenching, (2) thermal states and time-evolution in one-dimensional systems with short-range interactions, and (3) Lattice regularized field theories in (1+1)D. This work is accompanied by an open-source code that can be utilized to implement this method. This code is compatible with both MATLAB and Python, with numpy as the base numerical library. This code includes examples of implementing this method for multiple scenarios, such as the Bose-Hubbard dimer and lattice regularized phi^4 field theory. This code can be found at https://github.com/luca-abiusi/tn_tmbc_quench. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces. We illustrate the versatility of our method by applying it to a specific surface defined by a second-order partial differential equation and demonstrating how its asymptotic behavior can be determined through a series approximation that enables us to achieve the optimal Vinogradov bound of $\sqrt{19}$. We believe that our approach has the potential to be useful in a broader mathematical context. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, drawing on the information about submodules and their lattices. Given the lattice of submodules of one component and knowing that the lattice of submodules of the given module is isomorphic to its sublattice consisting of join irreducible submodules, we can construct the latter by identifying all submodules of the known component that contain a specific quotient module of the given module. This approach is demonstrated through examples, including a module whose lattice of submodules comprises five elements and cannot be constructed using Stanley's method, as well as a module with no join irreducible submodules other than the module itself. This implies that there are modules for which determining all join irreducible submodules is necessary in order to construct their lattice of submodules. This paper also introduces a new notation to facilitate the discussion of submodules and their lattices. This notation involves using the colon module $\Gamma$:\_ to define a sublattice of the lattice of submodules of $\Gamma$. This sublattice consists of those submodules of $\Gamma$ that contain a specific quotient module, and can be thought of as a "sublattice" of $\Gamma$ itself. This concept is then applied to the module $\Gamma^{(r)}$, which is isomorphic to the direct sum of $r$ copies of the module $\Gamma$. This means that for a module $\Gamma$ that has no module composition multiplicities, the lattice of submodules of $\Gamma^{(r)}$ is isomorphic to the lattice of submodules of $r\Gamma$, where $r\Gamma$ is the module obtained by adding the composition factor $r$ to the module $\Gamma$. This paper also discusses the relationship between the lattice of submodules of a module and the lattice of submodules of a module obtained by adding a module composition multiplicity. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. The code is available at https://github.com/ghulghul/CoImitationLearning.

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. Furthermore, a notable improvement can be observed when the action space is reduced without changing the vocabulary, as validated by multiple metrics including BLEU scores, semantic similarity and human assessment. Our research discovered that initializing the final fully connected layer with a layer that generalizes action similarities resulted in substantial RL performance gains, enabling it to tackle large action spaces efficiently. Which is especially relevant for NMT as its action spaces are inherently large. We've made the code available online for public access.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. The resulting formula for these energy flux distributions is straightforward and only depends on the electron temperature at the solar surface, which we determined as about 12500 Kelvin, also based on readings from the solar surface as recorded by instruments on board the Solar Telescope of the Advanced Solar Observatory in Mexico. This finding is significant because it tells us that the energy flux that can resist solar gravity and influence the solar plasma near the surface and in the wind, varies little with time and is mainly determined by fundamental characteristics of the sun rather than any temporal variations. The resulting model for energy flux distributions also enables the efficient removal of protons that can reach the solar surface and influence the solar plasma and wind in the inner heliosphere, which in turn allows for simpler models of the solar wind and plasma near the surface and in the wind. Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt a model trained on one domain to another, making it difficult to transfer knowledge to new, unknown domains. In response, researchers have developed domain adaptation techniques that enhance the adaptation of speech-emotion recognition models in real-world situations by counteracting the need for vast amounts of data from the target domain. While these techniques yield promising results, the challenge of overreliance on perfect annotation tools persists. To address this issue, a deep learning-based reinforcement learning framework is presented that adapts a pre-trained model on its own, eliminating the necessity for expert annotations. Initially, the model is instructed to minimize the discrepancy between the training and desired behavior. Next, a critic network is used to rate the model's performance, and a combination of three reinforcement learning techniques—policy optimization, value function-based optimization, and multi-objective optimization—is employed to guide the model towards the desired outcome. The framework is applied to a real-world application, speech-emotion recognition, and the results demonstrate significant improvements over conventional training methods. Additionally, the model's ability to navigate multiple objectives enables it to excel in situations that deviate from the training domain. Experimental analysis uncovers the relationship between the model's performance and various hyperparameters, facilitating optimized domain adaptation. The proposed framework surpasses state-of-the-art domain generalization speech-emotion recognition results and establishes a new benchmark for future research. A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified. In this model, the occurrence of acoustic emissions is linked to the sudden release of adhesive forces between the peeling surface and the tape, and the associated signal amplitude is determined by the instantaneous coefficient of friction. A non-linear relationship between the peeling force and the traction velocity is also identified, which has important implications for understanding the dynamics of many systems, from the human brain to financial markets, where similar non-linear interactions govern deterministic chaotic patterns in vast arrays of interconnected components. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures. This may have implications for certain non-perturbative renormalization group four-dimensional Yang-Mills theories, particularly in the near-conformal regime often encountered in certain finite temperature scenarios. This work extends and modifies previous research on the Yang-Mills-aether theory, particularly the non-abelian field strength tensor term, which was previously found to be incompatible with the renormalization group when analyzed within (3+1)d.

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts. Ultimately, it becomes apparent that this approach can be employed within more sophisticated models, such as the CEV model, by employing a change of measure technique known as Girsanov's theorem. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. This result can be achieved through a fair queueing approach, where opportunities are awarded based on an individual's socioeconomical status at the time of application. This dynamic and sophisticated model shows that giving preference to those with lower socioeconomical standings can lead to fairer and more efficient outcomes, challenging traditional merit-based approaches and highlighting the significance of considering an individual's birth socioeconomical status as a legitimate factor in allocation decisions. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package can stream out large chunks of simulated data at the rate the data is actually acquired, allowing it to efficiently handle several gigabytes of data per hour of simulation. This tool is particularly well-suited for pairing with machine learning training algorithms that can quickly try out different systematic effects on large amounts of simulated data. This research was supported by the National Science Foundation.
