Our work delves into utilizing pre-trained language models, specifically BART, for word ordering without the intermediate step of selecting a syntactic parse tree. We demonstrate how employing BART can be an efficient option, outperforming state-of-the-art results achieved through parsers. We also conduct additional experiments to determine whether BART's capacity to excel at linearization tasks is a general feature of T5-based models, which should be a valuable insight for future guidance. We ultimately find that while T5-based models like BART do excel at linearization tasks, choosing the best model depends on specific evaluation metrics. These findings contribute a nuanced understanding of how pre-trained language models function in word ordering tasks. We also provide accessible code to facilitate further research in this area. For those interested in evaluating the generality of our findings to other models and tasks, we propose a suitable experimental design called "Model Decomposition Evaluation". This approach involves analyzing the individual components of various models to gain a deeper understanding of their functions and capabilities, which should be beneficial across a wide range of applications. Specially, we show how using this method can help uncover the distinct purposes of different T5-based models, which should be a valuable resource for anyone working with these models. We make our code available at https://github.com/ghruvoi/t5-decomposition-eval. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. The code for the proposed MD-CSDNetwork is available at https://github.com/ghr96/MDCSDNetwork.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. With over 500,000 unique users and nearly 35,000 entered contracts, our data shows that Forsage operated as an exploitative pyramid scheme that generated substantial profits for a small group of administrators while causing significant financial harm to the vast majority of its users. This research provides an in-depth look at a rare and transitory moment in the lifecycle of a pyramid scheme, one in which the underlying transactions are normally obscured from public view. This analysis can be applied to a broad category of blockchain-based pyramid schemes and helps explain the inherent difficulties in defeating these types of scams through legal means. This research was carried out by a graduate student at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. This work has no affiliation with MIT. This research aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion among cryptoeconomists studying blockchain-based pyramid schemes and provides an open-source simulator used in the analysis. This research was inspired by the work of Elinam, the creator of the Forsage game. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. A note is also included regarding possible future research opportunities with the help of spectroscopic data that could provide a more accurate analysis of the proposed clusters. A catalog of the investigated clusters' key properties is presented in the paper's appendix. A second appendix contains a detailed breakdown of previously undiscovered star populations found within the bulge's core. A third appendix discusses VVV-CL109 and VVV-CL112 in more detail, finding them similar to the galaxy's giant armpits' star clusters known as the 30 degree armpit and the inner armpit. A fourth appendix discusses possible future research with the help of the galaxy's bulge's RR Lyrae star patterns and the effects of light obstruction and gas reduction. In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for an accurate representation of power-law behaviors in data. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that utilize diverse types of tensors, allowing these networks to successfully capture the characteristics of power-law behaviors while adhering to the principle of efficient calculation. A concrete example of such a network has also been developed - one that closely resembles the holographic HaPPY pentagon code under the assumption that specific system parameters can be set to a particular small range. different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and

occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations is being used to model low-energy Balmer continuum and UV continuum flares from sunlike stars, which includes results for a superflare event experienced by AD Leo in 1985. A combined ground and space-based UV and optical flux dataset from the IUE, HST, and ground-based spectroscopy and photometry is utilized to predict the continuum flux of this event, which in turn suggests that the 1985 stellar flare of AD Leo exceeded the energy of any recorded solar flare, with a peak energy distribution that remains similar to solar flares but with a significant shift towards shorter wavelengths. This shift towards shorter wavelengths has important implications for assessing habitable exoplanetary biosignatures in low-mass stars' near-UV environments. With a growing archive of stellar flare spectra, it is feasible to model the continuum of near-Ultraviolet spectral flares, which in turn can be compared to actual observations, providing valuable insights for assessing the energy of solar flares and informing the analysis of exoplanetary transmissions in the near-UV environment. This research is being carried out in collaboration with graduate students at the University of Colorado Boulder. A comprehensive dataset of the 1985 stellar flare of AD Leo, along with the radiative-hydrodynamic simulation code used to model this event, is available for public access. This study is being supported by a grant from the NASA Exoplanet Science Institute. A related paper titled "Modeling the 1985 April 12 White-Light Flare of AD Leo in the Balmer Continuum" has already been published, which focuses on the modeling of Balmer continuum flares. A related paper titled "The Energy Distribution of a Giant Stellar Flare from the Balmer and near-Ultraviolet Continuum" has also been published, which provides a comprehensive analysis of the energy distribution of this event along with a comparison to the energy distribution of the biggest solar flare recorded to date. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from astronomical spectra in the Hubble Deep Field South region. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Code for SparseGAN is available on GitHub at https://github.com/nyuML/SparseGAN. We have also made an accompanying submission to arXiv for the NeurIPS 2020 Workshop on Adversarial and Generative Methods for Natural Languages. With its capacity for efficient training and high-quality generation, SparseGAN offers a versatile baseline for natural language generation using GANs. We have specifically appraised its performance on large-scale datasets like the WebText30 million-parameter model input. With some adjustments, SparseGAN has delivered outstanding results, setting new records on datasets of this magnitude as per the Text Generation Challenge. We have made detailed implementation guides and training advice available with the code release. We have an open invitation to collaborate and explore new possibilities with SparseGAN. We have specifically explored and rejected three key sparse coding approaches that are crucial to understanding our novel method. We have also presented a series of additional experiments to evaluate SparseGAN's robustness and versatility. With its unique combination of efficient training and high-quality generation, we believe SparseGAN offers a compelling and versatile baseline for natural language generation using GANs. I explore the potential methods for identifying evidence of interstellar origins in microbial life, focusing on comet and meteorite analysis, and examine the challenges of distinguishing their native life from foreign life introduced during impact events. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resources chosen, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model the probability of space occupancy, resource selection, and provides estimates of population density.  This new method yields models that can be evaluated and compared, along with standard diagnostics for model-estimated parameters.  We also investigated how capture-recapture models incorporating habitat selection functions, in the form of spatial capture-recapture models using telemetry data and resource selection functions, can be used to estimate the probability of space occupancy, identify preferred resources, and provide density estimates.  Notably, our results showed that density estimates obtained from capture-recapture models and models based on telemetry data alone were highly correlated, and that the capture-recapture models yielded the same estimates of density as models based on telemetry data alone, with minimal loss of information.  This finding is critical because it demonstrates that the more straightforward capture-recapture models can be used to estimate space usage, resources chosen, and population density in many cases.  On the other hand, our research highlights instances where the integrated capture-recapture models would be more appropriate, such as when the study area contains multiple sub-areas with distinct and known habitat types, as long as the models account for this structure properly.  We explored and validated this type of model, which we call multisection models, along with analytical tools for evaluating and diagnosing these models, and the capture data from which they are derived.  As an application, we analyzed data from a study on black bears in Colorado, which are known to inhabit various sub-areas with distinct habitat types, and used multisection capture-recapture models to estimate the density of these bears in each sub-area, found that the models varied little from year to year, and that the integrated capture-recapture models accurately captured the structure of space usage and the distribution of resources chosen by the bears. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. From a practical standpoint, we illustrate the practicality of this approach by applying it to a multilayer network consisting of two identical layers and solving for the global synchronization state, as well as unstable spatiotemporal patterns that can arise within it. All the relevant MATLAB code has been made publicly available. Lastly, our work builds upon a previous study that introduced the joint matrix representation and interlayer edge placement model, yet our approach differs in several key aspects. Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. This research is not intended to contribute historical information but rather to resolve this longstanding misconception among celebrated physicists and mathematicians. A key outcome of this study is a newly generated set of geometric identities, equivalent to those obtained by J.H.M. Wedderburn, using an alternative and more intuitive method. Additionally, it modifies the classical G.B. Airy parameterization of the Cauchy stress operator by replacing the Bianchi operator with the Einstein operator induced from the de Rham complex, effectively transforming it into a non-trivial anisotropic parameterization. All in all, this research demonstrates the inherent connection between the Einstein operator, the de Rham complex, and the differential module defined by a set of geometric identities. It also introduces a novel concept known as the "Einstein-Algebraic" operator, a non-trivial anisotropic parameterization of the Cauchy stress operator, distinct from the Einstein operator and the induced de Rham complex. It further discovers an anomalous algebraic truth within this operator, marking which marks a significant departure from the previously misunderstood historical fact. Lastly, it presents an alternative and simpler proof for a renowned identity known as the Wedderburn's formula. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. The environment is adaptable to different programming languages and offers an API for customization. This testing environment is an expression of our geometric testing theory, which is an abstract framework with both a conceptual and a computational component. The conceptual aspect of the theory is focused on the underlying principles and the geometric structure that it uses, whereas the computational aspect deals with the algorithms and the environment mentioned earlier. The theory and environment are suitable for a wide range of testing scenarios, including exploratory testing, the testing of safety and correctness properties, as well as the identification of code smells. It also offers a set of tools that can be used for state-based testing, which is a approach that is both automated and interactive. This approach is different from traditional methods of state-based testing that rely on the automatic generation of test cases and mock objects. This testing environment and the underlying geometric testing theory have been applied to real-world projects and provide free source code that is available for public use. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The accuracy of the algorithm is proven through a probabilistic technique that involves an intricate analysis of the round-by-round protocol execution from multiple perspectives, specifically from the viewpoint of an honest node participating in the algorithm and from the viewpoint of a malicious node that could potentially devise an optimal strategy to disrupt the protocol. The accuracy of the algorithm is guaranteed to be effective and accurate for a vast majority of the nodes, i.e. up to 1 - epsilon. If we were to consider a less stringent accuracy condition of being correct for at least a quarter of the nodes, then the algorithm would be capable of estimating the network size within a much larger factor of the logarithm of the network size, specifically the logarithm to the base two. It is worth noting that our algorithm is optimized to handle networks with a large number of nodes, specifically those with a size of n greater than 10,000, assuming the parameter delta is set to a very small value, i.e. 0.01. The algorithm we designed for estimating the network size also serves as a foundation for a broader class of algorithms that could potentially solve other problems in similar uncertain conditions. The algorithm we presented is efficient as it is decentralized, requires minimal computation and communication, and is uncomplicated in implementation, however, it is not the most precise algorithm available as it is designed to be optimized for large-scale networks at the expense of a smaller factor of accuracy. Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths for an approach lane at an
intersection. Specifically, a Negative Hypergeometric distribution models these
estimates, which are compared to existing parametric methods using real-world data
from probe vehicles. The findings suggest that the proposed nonparametric
methodology matches the accuracy of traditional methods used in the field study. 
The approach has a significant advantage in that it requires essentially no
initial data to set the parameters, making it an ideal choice for new
intersections with no existing probe vehicle data. The method's effectiveness
also extends to intersections with varying repeat patterns, making it a valuable
tool for transportation professionals seeking to estimate and manage traffic
conditions across the transportation network. The approach can be implemented
using the Negative Hypergeometric Distribution Queue Estimation Tool, a simple
combining algorithm for probe vehicle data. The method's efficiency in this
tool allows it to handle large amounts of probe vehicle data in a reasonable
timeframe, facilitating the integration of the approach into real-time
traffic signal control systems. The study further examines issues related to
probe vehicle data validation, countermeasure design, and the integration of
the approach into dynamic traffic signal control systems. The appendices include
further details on probe vehicle data validation, the NHD Queue Estimation Tool
source code, and an illustration of the approach's effectiveness in a real-world
setting. The proposed methodology has significant implications for the
estimation and management of traffic conditions and provides a valuable tool for
transportation professionals seeking to optimize traffic signal control across
urban networks. The approach's public availability on GitHub enables transportation
professionals to access the NHD Queue Estimation Tool, the combinatorial
estimation algorithm, and the validation and evaluation data, facilitating the
integration of the approach into real-world applications. The approach can be
used at intersections with varying traffic signal timings, further extending its
validity to a broad range of urban settings. The appendices include a review of
the literature on traffic state estimation, the description of the validation
procedure and the data used in the validation, the specification of the NHD
Queue Estimation Tool parameters, and the description of the NHD Queue Estimation
Tool source code and the data used

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be satisfied for both the metric and the extrinsic curvature. Our novel approach modifies the standard conformal decomposition by introducing a new factor that equalizes spatial and spatial-time components of the extrinsic curvature. This change enables us to employ a single set of conformal factors across both constraints. By combining this method with the standard Hamiltonian constraint solver using Gaussian normal coordinates, we successfully generate well-behaved geometric variables that satisfy both constraints. This strategy is particularly effective in reducing grid density near black holes and can significantly improve the effectiveness of boundary advancement methods. Our approach has been effectively applied in simulations of rotating black holes and binary mergers. In these simulations, we observed improved stability and a marked decrease in grid distortion. This method is particularly advantageous as it does not introduce any additional parameters that require tuning, making it a straightforward and useful modification for a broad range of numerical relativity simulations. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further validated. As the understanding and potential applications of these materials rely heavily on correctly interpreting magnetoelectric response results, our analysis highlights the significance of distinguishing between the anomalous Nernst and thermal gradient components in experiments, and we propose a characterization method to aid in this differentiation, ultimately providing a framework for analyzing these effects in similar antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials. Lastly, our results on Mn$_3$NiN thin films, which exhibit both large anomalous Hall and Nernst effects, offer promising prospects for their use in technological applications. All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is exhibited within a probabilistic framework that was rigorously introduced by Rhodes, Vargas, and the first author. A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived via a precise derivation of the Miura transformation. Notably, we demonstrate that the spin-three Ward identities, which embody the principles of higher-spin symmetry, are an inherent component of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This proof is supported by an explicit analysis of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda two-point function. This proof relies on an iterative approach that originated from an examination of the Liouville two-point function case. This method involves utilizing a combination of the Dubois-Violette-Schottlander that classifies non-negative roots, the Birkhoff orthogonality, and the Gram determinants to demonstrate that the Liouville two-point function is invariant under the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Lie algebra. This proof can be further extended to demonstrate that the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda four-point function also obeys the spin-three Ward identities. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address these limitations by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Our code is available at https://github.com/JincaiTheThird/DECENNT.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, our approach determines whether a detected moving object is likely a living being. We tested and validated this method on a subset of a large publicly available dataset, finding it to be 90% accurate in identifying biolocomotion. However, we encountered issues with low-resolution videos that could be improved, along with other potential enhancements to our method. A discussion on the types of biolocomotion and their corresponding detection challenges is also presented. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. Our research builds upon these existing solutions and introduces a new iterative algorithm for matrix inversion that combines the neumann series and the Newton iteration techniques. The resulting algorithm yields a straightforward implementation that can be optimized for better performance on the memory structure of GPU devices. Furthermore, our solution develops a set of parameters that can be used to control the precision and convergence speed of the algorithm, enabling it to be suited for a broad spectrum of applications. The neumann series parameterization, in particular, allows the algorithm to conserve memory by limiting the number of vectors used in memory, making it particularly valuable for models with limited memory access, such as embedded devices. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. This work contributes an in-depth analysis of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with correlated disorders, and suggests possible experimental realization of the topological Anderson phases in atomic or photonic systems. This work also predicts that mean chiral displacement can serve as a sensitive probe to identify the topological Anderson phases and zero-energy mode localization with tunable disorder correlations. This research further expands on previous findings for spatially uncorrelated disorders, and provides a suitable model for investigating the interplay between strong non-rigidity and strong disorder. This includes spatially uncorrelated and correlated Anderson localizations in one-dimensional systems. This research may also be applicable to other spatial dimensions. This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies. The application of the 1-parameter family of isogenies from rank 1 elliptic curves can be seen as shifting monodromy weights, which has implications for bound states and scattering amplitudes. The research utilizes the Weyl group symmetry of the Coxeter-Dynkin diagram associated with the Feynman parameter triangulation to demonstrate that the curves' configuration corresponds to a super-symmetric (SSYM) configuration, which aligns with (non-holomorphic) Jacobi forms and ranks 1 elliptic curves, respectively. The study of Baikov parameters in their comprehensive form reveals a more intricate curve, but one that can be understood through the lens of rank 1 elliptic curves and their isogenies, which allows for the recovery of the original, simpler curves. The parameter configuration can be seen as generating family trees of isogenies, offering a new, geometric interpretation of the Baikov parameter approach. The research shows that the curves' relationship via isogenies enables the curves to share monodromy weights and bound states, which can be found using the 1-parameter family of isogenies from rank 1 elliptic curves. The study predicts that double-box integrals at any loop order will systematically exhibit these properties, which are characterized by the presence of (non-holomorphic) Jacobi forms and ranks 1 elliptic curves, and their isogenies, with the curves defined by an explicit set of cut conditions. The proposed approach can be applied to other sunset integrals at any loop order, provided that the curves inherently belong to genus one. The research offers tools for directly deriving the curves' invariants, which can be used to compare and contrast different approaches, with the goal of better understanding and simplifying the genus one geometry associated with these integrals. This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The results are implemented in the computer code "FeynHiggs", which provides predictions for the magnitude and phase of the Higgs boson field, as well as the rates for individual Higgs production and decay processes. The implementation is valid across a broad range of energy and momentum scales and is a crucial tool for interpreting LHC data within the MSSM with complex parameters. The contribution discusses the approach to calculating the magnitude and phase of the light and heavy Higgs bosons, with a focus on the impact of complex parameters on the results and the corresponding predictions for the phases of certain Higgs boson fields. Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle especially in decentralized systems. This issue is particularly pronounced when context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing two new algorithms, Context-Oblivious Upper Confidence Bound (CO-UCB) and Context-Oblivious Empirical Bayes (CO-EB), that effectively manage large context dimensions without utilizing the context information. This allows a central decision maker to make decisions without the need to share context, reducing communication costs. We establish regret bounds for both CO-UCB and CO-EB with respect to an ideal teacher that knows the distribution of contexts. We also derive a lower bound to demonstrate the optimality of our regret bounds. Additionally, we provide a context distribution condition that, together with known constraints, enables us to obtain our primary regret bounds. This condition can be satisfied by various distributions including the uniform distribution. We demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithms with numerical experiments. Focusing on wireless applications, we also consider a related exploration-constriction mechanism where we derive a new pseudo-regret bound. This bound is then utilized to extend the results of our main algorithms to the pseudo-regret setting. We believe our results can be applied to various decentralized systems, not just wireless applications. All the algorithms, proofs, and numerical experiments mentioned in this paper were implemented using the PyDCBAND framework. All the code along with the generated figures is publicly available. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as contradictions to binary power control generally being near optimal in everyday, non-long-term scenarios. A new category of networks, those exhibiting long-term extremal behavior, are also introduced with binary power control yielding the same gain values as in general contexts. A key part of this research also involves a binary power control gain characterization, providing a novel specific GDoF gain value of $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ for any number of $K$. This paper presents an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. It incorporates updated formulas for calculating particle collisions and interactions with the flow, and employs a predictor-corrector approach to solve the Ordinary Differential Equations describing particle dynamics. It is shown that our algorithm can recover the results from previous studies using a fixed time step, and significantly improves the computational efficiency of simulations requiring varied time steps. This is demonstrated in simulations of single particles falling through flow, as well as settling and collision scenarios involving thousands of particles. Our method has the potential to greatly accelerate particle-resolved simulations of complex settling and collision scenarios with large populations of particles, among other applications. This algorithm has been implemented into an open-source numerical solver called ESPResSo. This research was financially supported by the German Research Foundation DFG. This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$. One approach builds upon an earlier finding by K. Berzlowski and A. Strauch, which showed for any $n\geq 4$ there are pairs of $a$ and $b$ such that $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$. The second method of proof expands upon an earlier result by J.A. Panda and A.K. Swain, which stated for any $n\geq 3$ there are pairs of $a$ and $b$ such that $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$. Notably, one of the proofs presented offers an even broader existence guarantee, covering all odd primes $p$ and their powers $p^n$ in the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$.$\cup$2023IEEE. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached its desired jumping height in 0.4 seconds, and maintained a safe body angle. To enhance the optimal height achieved in a single jump, a gradient-based optimization algorithm was used to adjust the robot's leg position. This led to a 1.5 times increase in the height achieved. To replicate a more complex terrain scenario, the ground's configuration was modified to include a step. This forced an alteration of the feedback controller and the feedforward forces. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model, utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks and does so at a much faster pace than existing methods. We put our approach to the test on three distinct information networks and the results show that our model not only outperforms the current standard but also manages to strike a balance between the precision of its representations and the speed of their generation. These improvements make our model an ideal choice for the demanding requirements of web-based applications. We also make available the code for our model, HDFM, on GitHub.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in many quantum annealing applications, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can significantly enhance the effectiveness of quantum annealing. To demonstrate this concept, we conduct a quantum quench simulation of a single-qubit exact cover problem and successfully reproduce the annealing gap's behavior using this approach. This successful replication can be expanded to multi-qubit systems like superconducting spin arrays, offering a potentially valuable means of addressing the notoriously difficult challenge of identifying localized errors within these systems. Lastly, one of the most prominent issues in quantum annealing applications - error rate - can be extracted from the quench dynamics and provides a physical explanation for the occurrence of the annealing gap. This study is accompanied by a supplementary document containing a detailed explanation of the neural network used in this study.

Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
plausible ordering pattern. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped, $p$-type
superconductivity. 
Interestingly, strong screening can also yield an unconventional $d$-wave
ground state, further differentiating infinite layered nickelates from other
self-doped materials. 
These findings are obtained through a combination of exact diagonalization,
T-matrix approach, and a loop-summing fluctuation exchange (FLEX) method. 
This one-band picture provides valuable insights into this class of materials, 
and our results are consistent with existing experimental data, requiring 
further investigation. 
Infinite layered nickelates represent a novel opportunity to explore the 
interplay between screening, interactions, and self-doped superconductivity, 
and our work here is an initial step towards that goal. 
This one-band picture may also be applicable to other $3d$-electron based
materials with similar infinite layered structures, such as rare-earth
cobaltates. 
Our results suggest that the interplay between the T-term and the FLEX part 
is crucial in obtaining the correct ground state, a finding that may have 
implications for other correlated electron systems. 
Infinite layered nickelates offer a unique setting in which to explore 
this issue further.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit.  While this behavior could be displayed through relativistic models of dense matter, it's not a universal trait.  Quark-star models, which establish a connection between diquark interaction lengths and the conformal behavior of sound velocity, are a specific example.  The analysis of four strange quark stars shows that their density properties align with the conformal description expected in quantum chromodynamics.  This alignment supports the notion that matter within these stars is composed of strange quark matter, and also provides insight into the minimal interaction required for strange matter's negative pressure.  This interaction extends over a range of 10-100 megelvolts, which is consistent with earlier predictions.  The possible interaction lengths for diquarks are estimated to be around 0.5-1.5 fermi.  This study's results are a critical test for strange hadron cluster models, and our findings suggest that the density properties of quark stars are a direct outcome of the characteristics of quark hadron phase transition.  This study's findings also shed light on the interplay between the strange hadron cluster's condensate and the diquark interaction. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring a specific radial extent and is influenced by the characteristics of their particles. To study the VSI, a non-self-gravitating model of a particulate-pro rich upper region and a disk mid-plane is considered. By examining the effects of particle properties such as density and optical width on the VSI, our research reveals that an increase in these properties generally enhances the stability of the model. This outcome is attributed to increased heat generated by particle interactions, thus raising the temperature and reducing the radial entropy gradient. This result is consistent with previous findings based on numerical and analytical data. Additionally, our research shows that the VSI is unlikely to occur in the outer regions of disks, specifically in areas beyond 10 AU, where the conditions are favorable for particle growth. This phenomenon is known as the "cool disk" model and our analysis supports its occurrence. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/Co2C.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes that contain representative and diverse data. A novel random walk learning algorithm is proposed, along with two variants, to tackle different settings where the nodes are semi-supervised or unsupervised. The proposed algorithm ensures that each node participates fairly, reduces statistical disparities, and provides convergence guarantees. The results of our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in both homogeneous and heterogeneous graph settings. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  Key assumptions about this analysis and possible avenues for future study are discussed.  Suggested policy implications include expanding access to court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation.  The study utilized a large sample of over 30,000 offenders and accounted for various individual-specific factors including age, sex, ethnicity, residence, education level, employment status, whether or not the offender had a prior conviction, the type of crime committed, whether the crime was committed against a person or property, and the offender's mental health treatment needs as required by a court-ordered evaluation.  It also controlled for county-specific factors that could influence an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The analysis of these factors and the outcomes they produce provides valuable raw material for further study.  A preliminary cost-benefit analysis of the data has been performed but there are numerous possible ways to expand and refine this analysis including but not limited to incorporating the costs of incarceration for those who commit more serious crimes, accounting for the tax benefits which result from lower levels of future crime, and estimating the decrease in future crime with models that do not rely on a linear assumption.  Possible avenues for further study on this topic and the results it produces are also discussed. it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels accurately. To this end, we use
a novel interpretable graph neural network approach that localizes disordered atoms
at the molecular level for oxides, offering both precise and efficient disorder
predictions with a way to identify problematic atomic configurations. We apply
this methodology to determine the accuracy of classical and quantum molecular 
dynamics simulations and investigate the entanglement and lattice disorder effects 
on Al-doped SrTiO3. The results show that this paradigm offers a valuable 
insight into where and why atomic disorders occur, and as such, an excellent 
tool for materials researchers, beyond just precise disorder predictions. The
code for this research is available at https://github.com/material-gnn/ROX. The
data used in this research is publicly available at https://materialsdata.coda.org.

It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss, with a subsequent discussion on sampling theory and the asymptotic behavior of $\hat{\theta}_i$. We also discuss some challenging cases and potential future directions. We conclude by analyzing the asymptotic behavior of the GMLEs for the mixing distribution parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ and derive a new result that can be compared to a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956). Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. This proof is accomplished through establishing that $P$ has injectivity properties when paired with certain other operators, specifically when acting on functions with specific vanishing properties along lines or points of $M$. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a novel strategy that significantly boosts transcription results. We used a modified alphabet to incorporate more accurate pronunciation, leaving other model parameters unchanged. This simple yet effective method showed a 38% gain in data-efficient settings. We further customized the model to attain outstanding results, taking advantage of a coarse-to-fine architecture and linguistic characteristics. Notably, our Czech system based on a pre-trained English model ranked first in the Librispeech transcription competition. Our work's versatility is illustrated through successful application to historical texts. We made all our code and data preparations publicly accessible.

In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, released as part of this study. Our method achieved significant gains over a variety of baselines, including pseudo data generation approaches. Code for this research is available at github.com/salestock/FewShotGEC. The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, yield equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms for allocating one or many goods result in a state of mutual stability that is characterized by being fairly allocated. Our study reveals that, when allocating one good, there are mechanisms that yield a state of mutual stability that is characterized by being fairly allocated for any possible scenario. In contrast, when allocating many goods, there are scenarios in which there are mechanisms that yield a state of mutual stability that are not characterized by being fairly allocated, as we can identify instances of its kind. Notably, one of these instances is notable where the set of fair equilibria aligns with the set of efficient allocations that are envy-free. Our investigation also delves into various established approaches, demonstrating that under certain conditions, there are mechanisms that yield a state of mutual stability that is characterized by being fairly allocated for any possible scenario. We discuss some open problems about fair allocation that are yet to be resolved. All the relevant information for this investigation can be found at https://c2k20.github.io/. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/c2k20/Fair-Allocation. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. The anomalous distribution of its star-forming regions in UGC 8839 also offers a contrasting perspective on the dynamics of its type of galaxy, one that's typically characterized by an overabundance of star-forming regions. The resulting stable state, marked by minimal star formation except in its outer disk, suggests a "memory" of its distant interaction with a small spiral galaxy. The findings presented in this research were obtained using a variety of observational data including the Hubble Space Telescope, the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, and the ASTRONOMICAL OBSERVATION DATA SYSTEM (APOD). The unique features of UGC 8839 are further underscored by the incidence of similar HII regions in other spiral galaxies, indicating they may serve as indicators of a galaxy's dark matter properties. The research reported here highlights the rarest stage of the response of a galaxy disk, one that's hyper-stable on a grand scale, and the accompanying figures illustrate the extent to which UGC 8839 exceeds this norm. The interactions that gave rise to the unusual dynamics of UGC 8839 are consistent with a rare, three-body gravitational interaction, and the resulting state of the galaxy may serve as a standard for comparison with other spiral galaxies that have experienced similar interactions. The research presented in this paper is relevant to a broader field that includes studies of galaxy interactions, three-body gravitational interactions, and the properties of dark matter. The unique features of UGC 8839 are made manifest through the interactive research tool called Aladin, which allows for a dynamic exploration of the galaxy and its surroundings

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. Although our lattice data show patterns consistent with TPA (tree-level chiral perturbation theory) at very low masses, they deviate from it as the quark mass increases. This discrepancy is found to be more pronounced when examining correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark. Our lattice data also reveal that the effects of these correlations become significantly weaker as asymptotic properties are approached. This study's outcomes are crucial for guiding future studies aimed at comprehending the fundamental characteristics of hadrons through the analysis of lattice data with the aid of chiral perturbation theory. This research was conducted as part of the RBC and UKQCD Collaborations' projects.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/hananka/SIT.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Specifically, our 2D implementation achieved a mean surface normal orientation of 32.05 degrees, compared to 29.87 degrees for BHH, the 3D implementation showing a similar improvement. Additionally, our approach is computationally efficient, enabling real-time tumor tracking during radiotherapy treatments involving megavoltage images. To apply this model in practice, we provided a concise code utilizing TensorFlow, along with a dataset of registered brain images for training and testing. Moreover, we outlined a straightforward protocol for preparing megavoltage images for use in this model, including removal of patient identifiers and alignment with a standard brain template. To demonstrate its practical utility, we conducted a simple study on 3D brain image registration, utilizing 50 different brain images with known orientations, showing that our approach accurately predicts surface normal orientations with minimal variance. These positive findings suggest that Convolutional Neural Networks can effectively align megavoltage images, offering a practical solution for radiotherapy treatments and research involving these images. All code and datasets used in this research are available for public use.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that the instantaneous non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows a particle to acquire knowledge of the measuring device used to observe it, thus solidifying its'spooky' reputation. This finding's generality is ensured by our results, which apply to all possible scenarios, including those involving single-particle entanglement with itself. This achievement is made possible by our innovative use of the steering criterion, which enables us to demonstrate the reality of the non-local, instantaneous acquisition of information about the measuring device used to observe a single particle. This achievement in turn allows us to gain insight into the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics through the analysis of the instantaneous non-locality of single-particle entanglement.
