A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Experimental results demonstrate the potential risks of overestimating model complexity and offer guidelines for optimal GMM construction. Codebook construction and feedback algorithms were implemented on typical FDD baseband processors, with potential integration into 5G NR standardization. The approach can be applied to time division duplex (TDD) systems with pilot-based channel estimation, further expanding its utility. The research delivers novel codebook construction, feedback transmission, and receiving algorithms, as well as comprehensive experimental results, providing a foundational framework for future exploration and standardization discussion. The proposed method can be adapted for use in a range of scenarios, including but not limited to 5G NR TDD. The code developed during this project is available at https://github.com/yanghaoNJU/GMM-Codebook. The GMM-based codebook and receiving feedback encoding algorithms presented can be found under the directory Code/Algorithm, with MATLAB implementation of TDD system codebook and receiving feedback encoding algorithms located in Code/Algorithm/TDD. The research was supported by the National Key Research and Development Program of China (No. 2020YFB1406300) and the Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 62071057). The authors also acknowledge funding from the Jiangsu Province Key Research and Development Program of China (No. KBK20001). The proposed approach can be expanded to use machine learning-based codebook construction, as well as to adaptive codebook selection, with potential integration into standards and platforms such as 5G NR FDD, TDD, LTE FDD, TDD, NR-RRC, LTE-RRC, OpenAirInterface, srsENB, and Small Cell LTE. The research delivers a novel codebook construction, feedback transmission, and receiving algorithm, with the code developed available at https://github.com/yanghao

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 25% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 12% fall into nuclear star clusters. We estimate the remaining remnants in these locations could give us 24 decompression events and 12 direct mergers with total event rates of 0.02yr^-1 for decompression events and 0.006yr^-1 for direct mergers. Our predicted events would have total chirp masses of 26.1 solar masses, and are likely to be heard by the veto system of LISA. Our work highlights the potential for advanced gravitational wave detectors to gain insight into the universe's earliest populations, and stresses the importance of considering the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure. Our findings also suggest that LISA could discover a new class of merging binaries composed entirely of anti-matter. Our study further highlights the possibility of LISA discovering gravitational waves from binary remnants in the centres of dwarf galaxies. Our approach could be applied to a wide range of early universe scenarios formed by the movement of binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure. Our research was supported by the Australian Research Council. Our findings are consistent with results obtained using a fully hydrodynamical simulation of the early universe. Our study highlights potential discoveries that could be made by the Big Ripples project. Our research identified the key factors governing the development of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters and showed that the likelihood of mergers of these remnants is highly sensitive to the temperature of the early universe. Our study also found that the events involving these remnants would have total chirp masses far exceeding the typical values of the Big Ripples project's sample of merging binaries. Our analysis indicated that the events involving the remnants in the centres of galaxies would have total masses well above the LISA detection limit and our findings could be applied to a wide range of early universe scenarios formed by the movement of binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. These findings have important implications for the design of secure wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate its capabilities, we established three short-level text-based game courses and discovered that TextWorldExpress can efficiently evaluate virtual agents on a broad range of tasks, including those requiring multiple days by the original simulator. 
The accelerated simulator is accessible online at textworldexpress.org. 
Its influence extends beyond the text-based gaming community, offering a valuable template for users who manage and operate complex interactive simulations. 
Our findings also highlight areas where further optimization is possible for other widely used text-based game challenges, such as Hanabi, by identifying and applying various relevant optimization strategies. 
Our research is distinct from numerous recent publications that focused on developing virtual agents, rather than enhancing the text-based game simulator. 
One notable example is our own work, called TextSpiderAgent, which successfully conquered multiple challenging text-based game challenges, including some that TextWorldExpress has a hard time evaluating efficiently. 
Despite its limitations, TextWorldExpress provides a robust platform for evaluating virtual agents on multiple short-level text-based game courses, offering a useful tool for users who only need a simpler version of the simulator.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks capable of handling real-world data in video recognition. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for high-speed computation. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size and demonstrating substantial speedups on a customized hardware platform. Moreover, the hierarchical tensor decomposition-based FDHT-LSTM model exhibits superior accuracy in video recognition tasks, surpassing the RoI-Net baseline model in many cases. With its integrated algorithm and hardware design, FDHT-LSTM offers unparalleled flexibility to scale from software-only implementations on CPUs to customized hardware implementations, enabling efficient deployment across various real-world applications. This research also provides publicly available tools for the Hierarchical Tucker Decomposition algorithm that underpins the FDHT-LSTM model, facilitating its use for the tensor decomposition-based LSTMs in various sequence analysis tasks. The FDHT-LSTM model, along with the designed hardware accelerator and demonstration code, are all openly accessible on GitHub. This research addresses fundamental limitations in the scalability of LSTMs by integrating an algorithm and hardware co-design that enables energy-efficient and high-performance LSTM networks for real-world applications in video recognition, and its findings have far-reaching implications for the development of large LSTMs in other challenging sequence analysis tasks that involve high-dimensional data. The integrated design of algorithms and hardware presented in this work provides a versatile framework for unleashing the full potential of LSTMs in such applications. The Hierarchical Tucker Decomposition algorithm developed here is a generally applicable and efficient tensor decomposition technique that can be used in various co-designs of algorithms and hardware for energy-efficient and compact tensor-based models in various sequence analysis tasks. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field system, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the underlying quantum field system's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field systems, thereby solidifying the Weak Gravity Conjecture's foundation on principles of physics that are fundamental and inherently emergent. Last, it's demonstrated that this new conjecture, which we'll refer to as the Charged Conformal Conjecture, has the power to impose constraints on a conformal field system's properties, as illustrated by a specific example involving a massless scalar field. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The model offers actionable policy advice on the optimal design of redispatch markets, emphasizing the need for risk management tools that account for the risk profiles of market participants. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the planet's atmospheric composition, temperature, and movement through the use of infrared radiation. A distinctive and persistent polar stratospheric pattern of six-sided shapes, approximately 1000 kilometers in length, has been discovered surrounding the developing summer polar vortex in Saturn's northern hemisphere. This discovery is notable because it represents the first time a hexagonal shape has been found within the stratosphere and it offers a unique opportunity to observe the formation of the polar vortex in this region. The vortex, which appears to be analogous to those found in Earth's atmosphere during its own summer, is surrounded by unique temperature, circulation, and chemical patterns that are distinct from the surrounding areas and the planet's mid-latitudes. The study of this phenomenon will continue to guide scientists in their search for similar patterns of seasonal variation that occur on Saturn's sister planet, Jupiter. The extensive data collected from the Cassini spacecraft also enables a comprehensive analysis of the temperature, movement, and composition of the northern stratosphere, from the level of the atmosphere immediately adjacent to the polar vortex, down to 200 kilometers below it. The data collected from the spacecraft's radio frequency and magnetic fields instruments did not reveal any significant variations in the movement or magnetic properties of the atmosphere in the vicinity of the vortex. The primary mechanism driving the formation of the polar vortex remains unclear and there are several competing theories regarding which atmospheric process it is caused by, including the freezing of methane or ammonia or the result of a global temperature gradient that is influenced by the formation of the hexagonal shape. The study of the Saturn's northern stratosphere and the formation of the polar vortex in this region is significant because it provides a unique opportunity to test these hypotheses and it offers valuable insights into the complex processes that govern the formation of the polar vortex in the atmosphere of the giant planets. The extensive data collected from the Cassini spacecraft also enables a comparison of the temperature, movement, and composition of the northern stratosphere from the level of the atmosphere immediately adjacent to the polar vortex, down to 200 kilometers below it, with a level of detail that has not been previously achieved in any study of a giant planet. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary singularities in the derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that allows it to penetrate the boundary, ultimately facilitating an analysis of the dynamics occurring near the boundary and contributing to the optimal blow-up criterion. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. The reintroduction of lost phase information's value is not limited to x-ray scattering, as it applies to any modality that employs amplitude-only detectors. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. This methodology, in turn, can help address the methodological concerns and provide a foundation for a broader discussion of the Bayes factor estimation techniques used in this research, such as the application of objective utility functions and the assessment of Bayes factor sensitivity to the number of MCMC draws required for accurate results. This research was conducted as part of the BayesFactor project, which provides an open-source R package for performing Bayes factor analysis. This package, now in its third generation, includes an automated workflow that guides users through the Bayes factor estimation process and facilitates the assessment of Bayes factor reliability based on the variability of Bayes factor estimates derived from the application of bridge sampling and Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. This package is available for download on CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network, at https://cran.r-project.org/package=BayesFactor. on categorizing discourse markers based on their characteristics, our approach
explores their functional roles. We utilize a multi-step technique to assign
semantics to discourse markers, beginning with the creation of a corpus that
features discourse markers and their corresponding semantic functions. This corpus
serves as the foundation for training a machine learning model that can predict
the inherent properties of discourse markers. Next, an artificial neural network is
trained to perform the task of inferring the semantic functions of unknown
discourse markers. Our algorithm scours the internet for suitable candidates and
evaluates their semantic functions based on statistical patterns. We developed a
tool called DiscSense, an interactive command-line tool that allows users to
input discourse markers and receive the predicted semantic functions. Our tests

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors. A bipartite graph with a girth of seven and a certain degree of three in each side cannot be colored using six colors. This new example avoids the previous counterexample's characteristic of being cubic and adds another exception to the rule that an open series of graphs with a girth of two more than their maximum degree cannot be edge colored using the next integer greater than their maximum degree. This new series is made up of the odd numbers greater than six and includes the most recent counterexample given with a girth of six. A new approach is also found which can sometimes determine if a graph cannot be colored using a certain number of colors, by comparing it to another graph that has the same vertices and a different set of edges but is known to need more colors. This kind of transformation can be achieved by adding a specific type of cycle to the graph and provides an alternative way to prove some of the existing statements about the graph in question. This method is then used to find the mentioned example of a graph with a girth of seven. This approach originated from an earlier idea proposed by Kaul, Kishan, and Singhi in 2000. This paper also contains a statement that can be seen as a further extension to some of the existing rules about the edge coloring of a graph and may provide some background for the open problem that was proposed in 2018 by Faudree and Schelp, which is about the closed forms of some sequences of the cubic bipartite graphs with a girth of two more than their maximum degree. This open problem is to find formulas for the number of the colors needed to color these types of graphs and to investigate if there are any general patterns that can be used to determine these formulas. This is achieved by considering a specific and more general version of one parameter which is used in the formulas and to examine if both the even and the odd forms of the formulas are necessary. We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to determine whether they could converge on a Nash Equilibrium, the state of mutual stability where no player can improve their outcome by unilaterally changing their strategy. Our analysis focused on how different algorithmic components, including variation, selection, and genetic reproduction, influenced the emergence of a Nash Equilibrium. We found that both "soft" and "hard" selection mechanisms yielded Cournot outcomes closely resembling the Nash Equilibrium, whereas "hard" selection resulted in faster convergence. In addition, we found that higher mutation rates led to greater genetic diversity but hindered convergence to the Nash Equilibrium. Interestingly, we observed that the distribution of player outcomes could be bimodal, indicating some players consistently failed to reach the Nash Equilibrium even after the alleged convergence. This study provides a detailed examination of the complex interaction between the algorithm used and the game being played, offering valuable insights for future studies of dynamic processes in evolutionary and learning-based models of economic behavior. This includes an in-depth analysis of one notable limitation: the prevalence of "traps" that players become stuck in. We propose a new statistical method to assess the prevalence of these "traps" and offer empirical evidence of their widespread occurrence. In response to the widespread use of linear models in economics and the presence of "traps", we propose a non-parametric approach to modeling the relationship between the algorithm used and the game being played, and the prevalence of these "traps". This model enables the incorporation of both linear and nonlinear relationships, allowing it to handle the complex interaction between the algorithm and the game, as well as the presence of "traps". We apply this model to a variety of Cournot models and offer an empirical analysis of the prevalence of these "traps". The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratios primarily influenced by temperature rather than 
radial flow. Also, that the $\phi$/Kaon ratio remains steady in a "mass-free" 
environment, unaffected by final-state hadronic interactions. Detailed study 
of strangeness production, specifically $\phi$, Kaon and proton ratios to 
pions, reveals that they are consistent with those observed in proton-proton 
collisions and indicate that the "strangeness suppression" observed in heavy-ion 
collisions is a brief historical event that occurred at lower energy levels. 
Conclusively, extensive measurements of Xe-Xe collisions at the LHC provide 
precise and in-depth data on particle production and flow behaviour in nuclear 
reactions that will significantly contribute to better understanding of quantum 
chromodynamics in small and large-scale systems. Additionally, these findings 
will aid in testing current theoretical models that aim to explain origin of 
radial flow and initial geometric properties in colliding systems. S/π ratios 
observed in this study also pave the way for further analysis that will 
involve creating scaling variables that are independent of temperature and 
chemical freeze-out parameters, which in turn will facilitate a more 
precise and detailed analysis of particle production in Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions
that will significantly enhance the already substantial achievements of the 
ALICE experiment.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. This limitation is also supported by related research on migration behaviors within models. To better understand the underlying causes and dynamics of Santiago's 2019 riots, it is essential to consider historical ethnic and demographic patterns and current pre-riot social and economic statistics. These patterns and statistics reveal a paradoxical situation in which disorders' severity was highest in areas with minimal ethnic minority residency. Ultimately, this paradoxical finding may be attributed to a key factor not addressed in this analysis. It is also important to note that both models overestimated the disorders' duration when compared to actual figures. This project suggests possible future additions, including a review of academic literature on migration behaviors and possible data incorporation, such as crowd mobility patterns and demographic analytics, to enhance the models and facilitate a return to the original research question regarding disorders' duration. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. We also present a stateless, recursive algorithm for finding containment solutions using these methods and provide empirical evidence for the efficiency of this approach, comparing it against the standard method of translating to an automaton and FairKissatchean's solving method. We further discuss the implications of our research for the original problems proposed by Brzozowski and McAlister and Lee, Horning, and O'Dwyer. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals in real-time, limiting the capacity to design complex information fusion circuits. This research introduces EMA-VIO, a deep learning-based VIO architecture that leverages external memory in conjunction with attention blocks to enable the efficient fusion of multimodal information and signal processing. Experiments conducted using a moving camera showed that EMA-VIO achieves 2.5 times the accuracy of a standard LSTM-based VIO model and surpasses the state-of-the-art models in both accuracy and speed. Furthermore, EMA-VIO was successfully applied in a 3D printing robot that navigated in an unfamiliar environment with limited prior knowledge. The proposed external memory VIO architecture provides a versatile circuit that can be used in a wide range of localization applications involving complex, unknown environments. The code for EMA-VIO has been made publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ShangYuanZhao/EMA-VIO.

Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. This work also offers guidance on designing multiple qubit devices with stable and controllable SHOWS states. Besides SHOWS, our research yields related square-root semimetal (SRSM) and double Weyl (DW) state properties, providing a unified understanding and predicting unambiguous surface/state and bulk properties. This includes predicting specific anomaly pockets, robust hinge states, and distinctive double Fermi-arc surfaces that can be precisely engineered and directly observed. This knowledge can be utilized to develop multiple solid-state devices, from quantum computing and 2D exotic matter generation to unique anomalous phenomena in 3D bulk materials. This finding is also relevant to establishing a complete topological semimetal database. This study was conducted at Tsinghua University. This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. A non-iterative approach to the problem is examined and different hybrid mathematical formulations are introduced. Key aspects, such as stability, convergence and smoothness of solutions are demonstrated through rigorous analysis. Edge finite elements are employed to discretize the problem. Computational results, covering two- and three-dimensional cases and different types of missing data, are presented and show that the method yields accurate and smooth reconstructions. This research was published in 'Numerical resolution by the quasi-reversibility method of a data completion problem for Maxwell's equations' (SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 40 (2018), A105-A127). A priori and a posteriori error estimates are also established and analyzed. These studies provide a framework for solving a broader class of inverse problems involving the recovery of boundary data for partial differential equations. This work was previously known as 'Numerical solution to a mixed inverse problem for the time-dependent Maxwell equations' and can be found in (arXiv:1612.05395v2). A more recent publication in 'Math. Comp.' (MSC: 65-xx, 65Mxx, 78-xx, 78Mxx) further delves into the subject matter. A simpler approach to the problem known as the 'least squares mixed method' has also been examined and shown to be effective. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation Challenge, a new problem that arises in the context of a specific collaboration goal among institutions. Unlike in traditional federated learning, where institutions collaborate to achieve a common objective by sharing aggregated data, in FSAC institutions participate by contributing labeled data that are specifically selected to enhance the accuracy of a target model for a particular application domain. We present a comprehensive game-theoretic framework in which participating institutions determine the optimal subset of their data to contribute and a central authority is responsible for designing an effective selection strategy to guide their decisions. We also identify specific scenarios in which the optimal strategy is characterized by a straightforward and efficient approach, such as when institutions prioritize the accuracy of the target model, the security and privacy of their data, or their individual interests above all else. In these cases, participating institutions and the central authority engage in a variety of pure or mixed Nash equilibriums. We also outline numerical studies to illustrate the practical implications of FSAC in real-world applications. These experiments involve a central authority that aims to combine knowledge from a variety of institutions, each with their own unique expertise, as seen in tasks such as text classification, deep learning, and federated learning. We hope this work will help pave the way for a new era of collaborative knowledge construction in which institutions with diverse backgrounds and resources can work together to achieve a common goal. We believe this research is particularly relevant to a wide range of real-world scenarios, such as the collaboration mentioned above among academic institutions, as well as the integration of knowledge from various enterprises in a competitive business environment. These environments are characterized by institutions with access to unique data assets, each possessing its own distinct character, and with diverse motivations that drive their individual and collective actions. We propose a suite of feasible and efficient solutions to the problem of Federated Selective Aggregation Challenge that can be applied to a wide range of contexts, including but not limited to Ensemble Learning, Deep Learning, and Federated Learning, as seen in various numerical experiments presented in this paper. We also outline a series of open challenges and potential new names for the problem of Federated Selective Aggregation Challenge, including but not limited to the Challenge of Federated Data Weighting, the Problem of Federated Data Prioritization, the Challenge of Federated Selective Sharing, the Problem of Federated Data Triaging, and the Challenge of Federated Knowledge Construction. Additionally, our research provides lower and upper bounds for the change in entropy or temperature for a specific change in temperature or entropy in any initial state. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. This terahertz nanoscopy approach can be integrated with quantum processors to provide in-operation analyses, offering a promising future for enhanced stability and performance. This research was previously published in NPJ Quantum Information, volume 2.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions that could provide further insights into Venus's evolution and similar planets that may exist. Ultimately, understanding the complex interactions that have influenced Venus's atmosphere offers valuable lessons for detecting and studying exoplanets with similar conditions. This work is particularly relevant to the ongoing and planned missions studying the Venus system and analogous planets, such as the DAVINCI+, ESA's VERITAL+, and the LUVOK mission, which can provide critical information about the planet's evolution, its atmosphere, and its potential for hosting life. This research was conducted as part of the Venus research group at the Observatoire de Paris, and the results were presented at the 20th European Planetary Science Congress held in 2019 in Berne, Switzerland. This work is also part of the activities of the Venus expert group at the European Space Agency and was discussed at the agency's workshops in 2019 and 2020. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events are frequently used in various applications such as financial market analysis, biotechnology research, and network traffic studies. A non-linear Hawkes process with multiple branches is considered here. This process is unique in that it has feedback loops, which create reciprocal relationships between events of different types. Estimating the parameters of these reciprocal relationships is crucial in understanding and analyzing the mutual interactions and influences between events. We developed a new Bayesian estimation method that can be used to infer the non-linear Hawkes process parameters. This method, which is based on the theory of stochastic differential equations, provides an accurate estimate of the mutual interaction between events. We tested this method on artificially generated data sets of various complexities and found that it delivers high-quality estimates of the parameters and their confidence intervals. We also applied this method to a real-world data set consisting of 25 typhoon event types and found that it can capture the short-term and long-term fluctuations in the data and identify the event branches that contribute to these fluctuations. We were able to show this by analyzing the cumulative distribution functions of the refugee deaths caused by each typhoon type in Japan over a period of 67 years. We also demonstrated that a non-linear Hawkes process with feedback loops outperforms a non-linear self-exciting point process model in predicting the occurrence of events in the same time period. We were able to graphically visualize the refugee death event tree by analyzing the residual variance of the model and its relationship to the corresponding cumulative distribution functions of the refugee deaths caused by each typhoon type. We also found that the events that occurred less frequently than expected are located at the nodes that have a lower degree of branching and a smaller refugee death impact. We were able to further validate this model and analysis by conducting a Monte Carlo simulation study and an out-of-sample forecast analysis. As high-power laser pulse capabilities increase, the limitations of traditional solid-state optics due to their restricted damage thresholds pose significant challenges, making the investigation of plasma-based components more compelling. We propose a novel type of plasma waveplate based on a specific magneto-optical property when subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field, allowing it to function under extremely high laser intensities. This component can modify the laser pulse polarization while simultaneously increasing the peak power, which has been demonstrated numerically with simulations. It shows that a high-intensity linearly polarized laser pulse can be converted to a higher-powered circularly polarized pulse. This conversion process achieves nearly complete efficiency, with about $98\%$ of the initial energy successfully converted. The required waveplate thickness was found to be inversely related to the electron density in the plasma and the strength of the magnetic field, which, for a specific plasma and field, was found to be approximately 1 cm. This type of plasma waveplate can serve a pivotal role in the effective deployment of multi-petawatt laser systems. It enables the clean extraction of energy from chirped pulse amplification systems, allowing the generation of ultra-high intensity laser pulses with multiple petawatts. This can be accomplished through a simple optical arrangement that separates the desired central part of the pulse based on its polarization. This central component, which maintains the same pulse duration as the original pulse, can deliver an incredibly high peak power, as has been numerically demonstrated with simulations. It shows that a laser pulse with a peak power of one exawatt can be generated from a multi-petawatt amplifier system. We develop an efficient decoding method for correctable rank metric codes with a symmetric distance distribution, significantly enhancing existing decoding approaches for these codes, especially in regards to their optimal decoding thresholds. This improved decoding algorithm is under a second order randomness condition, which is a novel requirement for such codes. This novel decoding technique introduces two distinct decoding strategies: a successive cancellation method and a sliding window approach. Both of these decoders prioritize minimizing the number of rank metric measurements taken, which are costly to compute. This research also explicitly determines the second order decoding threshold for (3,5,1) rank metric codes, outperforming the previously reported decoding threshold in question. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that the optimal decoding threshold for Gaussian rank metric channels under a second order decoding condition equals the optimal encoding rate of the [12,3,8] rank metric code, which surpasses the previously recorded record. This achievement is noteworthy as it marks the first instance in which the optimal encoding rate of a rank metric code has been identified as the optimal decoding threshold for a specific channel. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observing its H-alpha and H-beta spectral lines, we found SN~2020jfo had a broader line profile than most other supernovae of the same type. Using the $M_{\gamma}$ parameter, which measures line profile width, we assigned SN~2020jfo a new category of Type II supernovae with large spectral line widths. Analyzing its progenitor star, we were unable to obtain a reliable mass estimate but ruled out low masses. SN~2020jfo also had a notably short plateau phase, from which we calculated its radial expansion velocity during this phase. Employing the analytical relations of McNamara et al. 2018, we modeled SN~2020jfo's radiated energy and mass of ejected material, finding these to be similar to those of other Type II supernovae with large line widths and massive progenitors with masses around 17 solar masses. This, along with its explosion mechanics, allowed us to model SN~2020jfo's light and velocity curves. From these models, we inferred that SN~2020jfo resulted from an explosive helium shell burning on a massive star's surface, and not directly from core collapse. This conclusion is also supported by the absence of strong helium lines in SN~2020jfo's spectra. This research indicates that SN~2020jfo adds a new supernova type to the existing categories, resulting from certain explosive processes on massive stars rather than direct core collapse. This phenomenon may have implications for similar supernovae that go undetected due to the lack of detailed spectroscopic analysis. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo's massive progenitor with a short plateau phase and large line widths challenges the current threshold mass for low-luminosity Type II supernovae, which is typically set at 15 solar masses. This research also highlights the significance of thorough photometric and spectroscopic analysis for understanding the explosion mechanics and progenitor characteristics of supernovae. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. A prototype of the MuLE optics has been fabricated and is being tested in our laboratory. With its compact design and excellent detection efficiency, the MuLE concept is highly suitable for a variety of astrophysical monitoring applications.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for obtaining the equilibrium configurations of rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, utilizing a conservative and semi-explicit Glover scheme, resolves the Einstein-Dirac equations for rotating stars and incorporates a rotational framework with proper treatment of Dirac's equations and Einstein's field equations in their full, non-linear form. Unlike traditional methods, we do not assume an a priori relation between the metric functions and matter fields, instead employing a two-pronged approach where the Allen-Bradley algorithm is used to solve Einstein's field equations for the composite Riemann tensor, and subsequently, the Einstein tensor is used to solve the Einstein-Dirac equations. This methodology allows for a wide range of rotational configurations by incorporating the Euler beta function within the distribution of specific angular momentum. By applying this method to static stars and polytropes, as well as rotating neutron stars, we have demonstrated its applicability and the resulting formulations are suitable for use in time-dependent simulations. Ultimately, this novel formulation serves as a foundational step for investigating the dynamic behavior of rotating stars under various perturbations and mass accretion scenarios. The developed code, known as GR21, is specifically designed for high-performance computing and our tests have shown it to be approximately 10 to the power of 5 times faster than a comparable pseudo-spectral method. The code has been successfully applied to obtain the mass-radius relationship for rotating neutron stars in general relativity and our results are in close agreement with prior studies using other methods. The contributions of this research are not only the novel formulations and numerical results but also the development of an efficient and semi-explicit conservative solver for the Einstein-Dirac equations that can be used as a starting point for future time-dependent and rotating star simulations. The code, along with the results from static and rotating neutron star configurations, is available online for further use and modification. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. More remarkably, we found that models trained with only a few hundred documents can achieve near-professional-level accuracy, exceeding the performance of models trained on much larger datasets labeled by human professionals. Our work offers a scalable solution for incorporating AI models that can handle a wide range of documents, without getting bogged down in the expensive and time-consuming process of large-scale human labeling. Our code is available at GitHub at https://github.com/google/selective-labeling.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational wave data, a task that can be efficiently accomplished using machine learning models. Our novel approach involves a two-step process where we first employ a convolutional neural network to categorize signals as mergers, and then use an additional neural network to determine the binary component type. Our results indicate that this approach can accurately classify signals from neutron star-black hole mergers with a signal-to-noise ratio of 12.5, a level that can be reached for future detectors like the enhanced design of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory. Moreover, this approach allows for real-time analysis that complements the Markov Chain Monte Carlo estimation used in parameter inference, enabling a direct prediction of electromagnetic output through the characteristics of gravitational waves. This prediction, in turn, facilitates focused electromagnetic observations that can be conducted in a more economical manner, reducing the number of sources monitored in real-time by an order of magnitude. Consequently, this is crucial for achieving an efficient electromagnetic follow-up with the next-generation detectors. Our code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/krishnasren/NSBH-classifier. This research was conducted as part of the 2019-2020 gravitational wave research projects at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. We used the LIGO Science Grid Computing Resource Manager for computations and the Open Source Gravitational Wave Detector Science Software (GWPy) for data analysis. The accretion of these objects by the stellar body could explain the recently observed episodes of rapid growth. By post-processing a prior simulation using a one-dimensional model, researchers found that material accumulating at the inner disk does not always result in significant accretion bursts on its own. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based automatic text summarization in a novel way to enhance the efficacy of our existing fake news detection system. By utilizing a condensed version of articles, our model achieves notable improvements in several evaluation metrics. When applied to individual articles, our technique achieves exceptional results, surpassing the current state-of-the-art in several metrics. Moreover, we introduce a new system that combines the individual article-based model and our original system, demonstrating a significant boost in accuracy over both individual components. Our code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/AhmedHamdy1994/TextSum4CRED.

A crucial observation in this analysis concerns the effect of spatial curvature, which, when considered, significantly impacts the probability of certain pattern formations emerging in these fields. It has been mathematically proven that fields with a certain level of curvature irregularity will inevitably exhibit specific patterns at larger scales. A key discovery also emerges from this study, which provides unique insights when compared to existing theories regarding random process smoothness and its relationship with generated patterns. Existing theories suggest that patterns will only emerge and increase in irregularity at infinite scales, in contrast to the curved case where patterns and increased irregularity emerge at a specific, finite scale. This research can be applied to a broad range of fields, including but not limited to, finance, biology, and geography, where researchers study complex, evolving natural systems and the mathematical principles that govern them. A key contribution of this study to the broader academic community concerns the development of a new statistical tool designed to measure the curvature of these complex systems, enabling a deeper analysis of these systems' evolving scales and the probability of emerging patterns and increased irregularity. This tool, known as the "curvature effect," allows for the prediction of the scales at which patterns will emerge and the systems will become more irregular, a capability that can be demonstrated through numerical data and real-world examples, including a randomly generated Gaussian field and a model based on the geometrically curved Menger sponge. This research also explores the relationship between the systems' irregularity and their scaling levels, discovering that it follows a distinct, linear pattern that can be observed through numerical data and real-world examples, such as the mentioned Gaussian field and Menger sponge. A key finding of this research, concerning the randomness of systems at infinite scales, reveals that it will necessarily become more curved and irregular at specific, finite scales, a concept that can be further expanded to a broader principle known as the "curvature theorem." This theorem states that systems at infinite scales will necessarily exhibit a particular level of complexity and irregularity, a characteristic that was validated through numerical data and real-world examples, including a model based on the Escher's staircase and a randomly generated Gaussian field. When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked alternative to conventional PCA due to its robustness in recent years. This study focuses on an under-explored version of rotationally invariant L1-PCA and develops an iterative optimization approach using proximal alternating linearized minimization and a form of extrapolation tailored to its two-block representation. Moreover, the algorithm is theoretically proven to converge linearly to a stable point, and this result is guaranteed to correspond to a minimum of the original problem when the damping parameter meets certain criteria. To support and validate the methodology, both artificial and real-world data were used in numerical experiments to illustrate the algorithm's performance. Unlike other variants of L1-PCA, the development of an efficient and linearly convergent solver for this specific problem offers promising potential applications, especially in large-scale machine learning settings where robust dimensionality reduction is critical. The development is specifically demonstrated through an analysis of text documents where topic extraction is susceptible to anomalies. The implementation is accessible through the open-source optimization framework, TFOCS. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels and selecting model-suggested labels based on contextual information. In successive experiments, we find that both machine-learning-trained models and human annotators whose decisions are guided by BERT tend to produce more consistent annotations. Furthermore, a significant reduction in inter-annotator disparity is observed when human annotators are guided by BERT. Ultimately, our findings provide a foundation for exploring the potential of assisted annotation tasks using neural models. For the sake of reproducibility, we present BERT-Assisted EMO20Q Annotation Code at https://github.com/ghrua/EMO20Q_BART.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

This demonstrates the capabilities of atomic interferometry in detecting the Meissner effect and expands on the range of applications for superconducting magnetic sensors that can now include finding very small cracks in superconducting materials. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for a broad range of developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout system that optimizes memory access for maximum cache efficiency, and a simple, unified API.  As a result, DynaSOAr enables easy and high-performance GPU programming for a wide range of SMMO applications, as demonstrated by our benchmark tests which show that it offers significant improvements over other popular memory allocators including tbb::malloc and std::malloc.  In particular, the allocators for global memory used in DynaSOAr achieved a 3 times speedup and a 2 times size reduction respectively over the default CUDA allocator.  Furthermore, our benchmark tests validated the efficiency of DynaSOAr's cache system and memory access optimizer, and showed that they can offer a 2 times speedup over less optimized versions.  To facilitate easy adoption of GPU programming for a broad range of developers, DynaSOAr provides a simple, object-oriented design with reusable modules that can be easily integrated into existing projects using its easy-to-use API. We made DynaSOAr publicly available on GitHub to meet this goal. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  These findings also highlight the importance of choosing the appropriate functional in the VASP code, and the need for accurate cell and atomic relaxation in 93-fold supercells.  We propose that Ti-defect centers could be created via a similar N-O bonding mechanism, and suggest possible experimental paths to verify our findings.  These include: leveraging near edge absorption fine structure, k-edge spectroscopy, or partial neutralization experiments.  These researchers believe that this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms and structures involved in doped TiO2, and could serve as a starting point for similar studies on other materials.  Further investigations into the charge and magnetic dynamics of these defects, as well as possible partial neutralization experiments, could significantly contribute to our understanding of this subject.  This could be achieved through a combination of theoretical simulations, experimental techniques, and comparison of the two. This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. The elastic potential of the LHC highlights a previously underappreciated capability of the collider, offering potential for discovering rare top-quark decays which cannot be detected through other means. This idea is well-suited for early operation at the High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider. 

# ElasticPotential_LHC
This GitHub repository contains the necessary information and code for the analysis described in the paper "Elastic Potential: A proposal to discover elastic production of top quarks at the Large Hadron Collider". This research was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy and the National Science Foundation. This code utilizes the "Elastic Potential" protocol which was developed in collaboration with the ATLAS experiment. This protocol makes public proton-lead and lead-proton data from the Large Hadron Collider for the purpose of analyzing forward processes. Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of an extremely intense linearly polarized laser on a thin, micrometer-scale target pre-heated by a thin layer of plasma. The results show that, when the number of generated positrons becomes substantial at intensities exceeding 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square centimeter, the produced positrons exhibit notable polarization properties. In fact, the polarization of the positrons can reach over thirty percent, with an accumulated charge exceeding 30 nanocoulombs, emitted with an enormous intensity of ten to the power of 12 per unit steradian. The degree of polarization is influenced by the angle of the emitted particles and their corresponding energies. The theoretical analysis is compared to simulations, demonstrating that the positron polarization exceeds 90% when the electron's energy approaches the critical value required for pair production, and that the degree of polarization decreases as the energy of the electrons and the intensity of the laser increase above this threshold. The findings suggest that solid-state targets may serve as efficient sources of polarized positrons, taking advantage of the strong field acceleration inherent to interactions between intense lasers and matter. The potential applications of these sources in physics and other fields are also discussed. The numerical data generated during this study has been compiled into an appendix for further reference. The results presented in this study were obtained using a specific simulation code, but the underlying physics is general and applicable to other numerical tools. The theoretical analysis employed a previously established model describing the polarization of emitted electrons and positrons, which can serve as a tool for interpreting future experiments and simulations. The study concluded by examining its own limitations and proposing several ideas for improving the efficiency and polarization properties of the positrons produced, including targeting surfaces with specific patterns of micro-roughness and utilizing circularly polarized lasers. The potential for these sources in physics and other fields is also discussed. The numerical data compiled during this study is presented in an appendix for further reference. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a remarkable 0.24°C root mean square resolution, a ±1.4°C inaccuracy, a ±3.4°C theta (long-term inaccuracy), a 1.06nJ conversion energy, and a 5.4mA average power consumption. Experimental results from 0°C to 85°C, 85°C to 125°C, and 125°C to 150°C temperature ranges revealed a minor non-linearity effect but required a non-linear calibration to correct for it. This non-linearity was mitigated by employing a specially designed look-up table based on a limited set of calibration data, thereby ensuring the sensor's efficiency and minimizing its memory footprint. A working prototype was also built to demonstrate the sensor's functionality in an adaptive voltage and frequency scaling system, featuring a simple yet effective dynamic voltage regulation mechanism, a frequency-temperature ratio conversion module, and a theta estimation module. The experimental results from this prototype in various scenarios are presented and compared to similar temperature sensors developed by other researchers. We've developed a 3-step protocol to address this issue and accurately classify skin cancer images. In neural machine translation, the attention model is typically applied between source and target sequences, enabling selective focus on source words corresponding to target words. However, research reveals that source-target attention alone fails to surpass the baseline without reinforcement training. To address this issue, we introduce a look-ahead attention model between the middle of the source sequence and the remaining generation process. Empirical evidence shows a significant improvement in metrics when using a partial look-ahead attention model. As a result, our method surpasses the baseline without reinforcement training. To further validate our approach, we conduct a range of experiments with different look-ahead positions and source-target masking techniques. Our results demonstrate consistent performance gains. To understand the underlying mechanisms, we analyze the search patterns of our proposed model and find it compares favorably to the conventional approach. To ensure our findings are robust, we conduct additional experiments on large transformer models and compare our method with state-of-the-art conditional masking techniques. To facilitate reproducibility, we provide the code and models used in our experiments. Our proposed look-ahead attention model offers valuable insights into the generation processes and provides a foundation for further research in controlled, natural-language generation. The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and key technology of grid computing. A translational perspective is shown to be comprised of three components: a problem can be expressed as an instance of a suitable abstract problem, there are efficient algorithms to solve this abstract problem, and these algorithms are implementable as a solving process. Within the context of grid computing, these abstract problems take the form of grid frameworks such as grids, clouds, and federated environments. Not only did a translational approach facilitate the rapid development of grid computing but it is also the underlying reason for the field's success. This success can be measured by the widespread adoption of grid technology in various real-world applications, including finance, transportation, and scientific research. A translational approach has the potential to drive practical applications across multiple fields, making it an important area of study for the broader computer science community.
