Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Our research utilized data from J/ψ decay into two photons, Lorentz structures of neutrino or dark matter interactions, and photon energy spectra in invisible decays. We established the J/ψ energy production threshold at 7.25 GeV for our analyses. Our results provide a baseline for future J/ψ sensitivity on certain energy scales and offer opportunities for (J/ψ, η; invisible) and (J/ψ, invisible; invisible) searches to significantly lower these limits. Our effective field theories are applicable to a broad range of initial states, including those with gluons and heavy quark pairs, and our research paves the way for studying light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter through J/ψ decay into visible matter. We outlined a strategy for setting up such searches at facilities like the Beijing Spectrometer III, the Crystal-Box experiment at the Beijing Electron Positron Collider, and the BES-VI experiment at the Chinese Accelerator Drive Institute. Our analyses highlight the unique discovery capabilities of (J/ψ, ) and (J/ψ, γ;) searches for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter at hadron colliders. Our research found that (J/ψ, γ;) searches are particularly effective for detecting dipole dark matter interactions with gluons and heavy quarks. We concluded that future J/ψ sensitivity on certain energy scales and (J/ψ, γ;) or (J/ψ, ) searches for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter at hadron colliders hold significant discovery potential with the ability to significantly lower the energy scales

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of multiple time series singular spectrum analysis components, each applied to specific functional data dimensions. By incorporating these components, we derive the multivariate functional autocorrelation matrix and innovation process, which are crucial for time series prediction and other tasks. We then investigate the theoretical properties of MFSSA, including the asymptotic behavior of the eigenvalues of the matrix containing the underlying process's covariance function. To facilitate practical usage, we develop an efficient algorithm to compute the MFSSA components. Finally, we demonstrate the efficacy of MFSSA and its components via simulations and real-world data applications. These include the analysis of multivariate functional time series data in finance, genetics, and climate science. With its broad implications, this work provides a new tool for researchers and practitioners to explore complex, high-dimensional time series data. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. A helical antenna with a smaller number of turns was added to achieve helicon mode at all magnetic fields, and it was found that this configuration allows for flexible control of plasma density and edge stand-off distance. These findings have significant implications for the design of future plasma sources for helicon-based plasma production. A comprehensive overview of the IShTAR facility, including its plasma source and helical antenna, as well as the analysis methods used in this study, can be found in separate papers published earlier. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA, alongside direct-kernel-based elastography estimation, to enhance lateral displacement estimation. Experimental findings, involving rabbit muscle tissue with an implanted cancerous growth, demonstrate the VSSA-based technique's capability in accurately estimating both axial and lateral displacements. Consequently, this technique's effectiveness in imaging a range of soft tissue types becomes evident, extending its potential to a broad range of clinical applications. Notably, VSSA holds promise for combining with other elastography techniques, such as differential elastic matrix estimation, to further enhance the accuracy of mechanical property estimation. By focusing on a suitably chosen simplicial complex, our algorithm is able to provide solutions to the clustering problem that are within a factor of $O(\sqrt{d})$ from optimal, where $d$ represents the underlying space's dimension. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale
stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment
into distinct regions. Within each isolated area, a separate, smaller pursuit-
evasion game is played to achieve a mutually beneficial outcome. Our approach
invites one group of agents to focus on navigating between different regions,
while others work together to collaborate within their respective domains.
We establish through simulation testing that our hierarchical model yields a
significant decrease in both the number of agents required and the complexity
of local games needed to resolve larger-scale stochastic pursuit-evasion problems. 
Our results demonstrate how a hierarchical design can produce scalable and
modular solutions in various stochastic grid world settings. Our code is available
at https://github.com/ghallam/Hierarchical-Pursuit-Evasion.

This paper uses the Effective Vector Boson Approximation (EVBA) to assess the outcomes of high-energy muon collisions, focusing on long-lived systems and rare decay processes. In particular, we find that the EVBA significantly excels at calculating scattering amplitudes for high-energy processes, though it falls short of the Monte Carlo method's accuracy in certain cases of rare decays. The EVBA is suitable for applications in low-luminosity colliders and can be applied to multiple processes, although it requires further development to handle certain rare processes and certain physics phenomena. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our results demonstrate that both isolated policy and dynamics model
approaches, and a hybrid of the two, are effective in finding the optimal
balance between exploring and benefiting from shared representations in multi-task
reinforcement learning. To our knowledge, this study presents the first set of
results exploring the use of shared learned dynamics models in multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Moreover, our analysis and findings on the
prevalence of catastrophic interference offer a clear understanding of these
results and provide a roadmap for future research on the topic. Our code is
publicly available at https://github.com/abhinavc2006/mmtmrln.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. By combining these results, we obtain three key consequences: the certainty that any formal system meeting specific criteria cannot be both complete and certain, the certainty that any such system cannot define the statement it cannot prove, and the certainty that any such arithmetic system cannot be both consistent and complete. These conclusions were all achieved by a single line of reasoning, and as such, we dub this finding the "Reunion of the Five". It is worth noting that all of these theorems and their combined forms have no bearing on the vast array of formal systems that employ a different kind of reasoning, known as intuitionistic logic. It is also worth mentioning that we have made no attempt to original contribute to these celebrated results, but rather set them side by side to highlight their interconnectedness. It is our hope that this unified proof will help provide insight and understanding into these seminal theorems. It is our further hope that this reunion of the five will serve as a celebration of the profound contributions made by Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser. It is our aim to make the concepts underlying these theorems accessible to a broad audience by using straightforward and simple language. It is our intention to offer a historical context for these results, as well as explore their connection to some of the most fundamental issues in the philosophy of mathematics. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. Throughout this discussion, we emphasize the critical role that symmetry plays in dynamical systems and the limited applicability of fractional-order systems to conserve linear subspaces as invariant sets. We conclude by reviewing some notable research that explores the relationship between fractional-order systems and geometric symmetry, including the existence of symmetries of odd dimensions and the nonexistence of invariant manifolds in fractional-order systems. We also discuss some open problems in this area, such as the identification of system parameters that define linear subspaces as invariant sets and the coexistence of multiple invariant subspaces in some systems. We propose a new classification for these systems based on the structure of their invariant sets and suggest potential methods for analyzing these systems, including the use of Lie group analysis and Melnikov method applications. We acknowledge the contributions of distinguished researchers, including Czech, Bajgerga, Guan, Li, and Liu, to the study of fractional-order systems and geometric stability, and we outline some future research directions in this field. We also provide a list of relevant acronyms and the solutions to some system dynamics based on linear subspaces used as invariant sets in some examples from the main text. We conclude by reviewing the key findings presented in this article. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This particular screen's velocity and orientation are also determined, offering further insights into the dynamics of the Local Bubble. This finding highlights the value of prolonged pulsar scintillation observations and measurements, capable of uncovering intricate details about the nearby interstellar medium. Furthermore, this discovery supports the complex geometry of the Local Bubble, a vast cavity in the galaxy. The data and analysis have been made publicly available on a dedicated website. The ongoing observation of the pulsar PSR B1133+16 and its surrounding screens provide valuable information for future studies, including a planned deep survey of the Milky Way's interstellar medium with the Square Kilometre Array. The extensive data set for this pulsar also offers opportunities for combining scintillation and pulse profile measurements, as well as for exploring transient screens that have been discovered. The analysis of the data has been discussed in three companion papers that focus on specific aspects of the observations. These include models of the screens, the distribution of scintillation patterns during the Earth's orbit, and the transient screens that have been discovered. The code used for the calculations and the data sets used for the analysis have been made publicly available on a dedicated website. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling sequential data along the frequency axis. To overcome this challenge, QPNet divides the pitch range into multiple narrow intervals, assigning a distinct neural network to each, with inter-network probability correlations established using an attention-based mechanism. The employment of separate networks enables better adaptability to diverse pitch patterns, while the inter-network connections facilitate the model's ability to learn sequential data patterns across the frequency axis. The evaluation of QPNet using the LJC Corpus and the VCTK Corpus demonstrates improved quality and pitch control compared to WN and other baselines, showcasing the model's effectiveness in addressing the limitations of WN and comparable performance to state-of-the-art non-autoregressive models on the MELD Dataset. Code availability: Quasi-Periodic WaveNet is implemented using the Tensorflow framework, with pre-trained models and demonstration notebooks accessible via Google Colab.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. To achieve this, we develop a trial-and-error, two-phase approach for you, the AI, to learn effective methods. In the first phase, we assess various ways in which the model can fail, then in the second phase, we test different solutions to sound source localization problems. Our approach is designed to determine whether the model can differentiate between correct and incorrect methods and if it generalizes to unknown images. To validate our approach, we created an extensive set of models and methods in failure spaces, demonstrating that the model successfully identified the sounds it could localize accurately and those it couldn't, and that these spaces are not interchangeable. This is shown through various analysis and experimentation, including evaluating the model on a subset of unknown images. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the model can efficiently learn the sound source localization task with minimal manual guidance, setting it apart from comparable models. To facilitate further research, we are releasing our dataset of trained models and failure spaces, which can be accessed through our website. This work was presented at the International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV) held in 2021.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. This inverse problem is considered under the assumption of a weak formulation of the structural PDE, allowing for different discretization methods to be employed. An approximation scheme is also developed to solve the inverse problem through a gradient-type method. This scheme's convergence is demonstrated through the stability estimate obtained. Computational results are presented to illustrate the behavior of this scheme. This research adapts methods initially presented in two separate studies. The uniqueness and stability results draw from [J. Hollan, Inverse Problems and Imaging, Vol. 9, No 3 (June 15, 2015), pp. 765-785], and the approximation scheme and stability estimate draw from [G. Bal, Inverse Problems and Imaging, Vol. 1, No. 1 (2006), pp. 3-18]. These methods have been adapted to accommodate the specific structure of the Kirchhoff plate equation and the structural acoustic PDE model. This research also contributes a result on the regularity of the solution to the direct problem, which may be of independent interest. A discussion is presented on the possibility of employing a control theoretical approach to solve this inverse problem. This research considers a one-dimensional structural acoustic PDE model, which serves as a simplification of the original problem. This simplified model's inverse problem is solved through a different method, which draws from the control theoretical approach. This research initially appeared in the form of an arXiv preprint on May 12, 2020, under the title "An Inverse Problem for a Structural Acoustic Interaction". This document includes an added section on the control theoretical approach, as well as a corrected uniqueness and stability result for the one-dimensional model, which was initially incorrect. When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  This particular gauge can be achieved through a direct variation of the standard Fierz-Pauli parameter $m^2$, allowing for a simple and intuitive interpretation of the $m^2$ term as a harmonic gauge choice.  This approach can be extended to the most general linearized gravity theory, suggesting that the harmonic gauge itself serves as an essential tool for analyzing the massive gravity theory at the linearized level.  Despite these findings, it is crucial to evaluate the impact of the harmonic gauge on the full nonlinear gravity theory, which can involve challenging problems of convergence and gauge invariance, given its non-linear nature.  This can be achieved through an alternative method using a perturbative expansion around the identity gauge, which enables a controlled analysis of the nonlinear theory while minimizing potential issues of convergence.  This approach allows for an explicit demonstration of the hyperbolic general relativity theory's stability in the vicinity of the flat space solution, thereby providing a linearized analysis as a special case.  This note is intended to be a concise overview of two previously published research papers that explored this harmonic gauge in the context of linearized and nonlinear gravity theory.  These studies revealed the harmonic gauge's distinctive characteristics and its capacity to yield five degrees of freedom in the linearized theory, as well as its stability in the nonlinear regime through a perturbative expansion around the identity gauge.  This note aims to guide readers through the development of these research papers with a focus on the key results and an overview of the underlying methodology.  This approach can be used as a starting point for investigating more general theories of the massive gravity type.
